title: Cypress task exposes arbitrary server-side configuration values
description: The Cypress Node task `GetFromConfig` accepts an arbitrary property name from the Cypress runner and returns the corresponding value from the server-side configuration. Any test code able to invoke `cy.task('GetFromConfig', variable)` can probe and retrieve configuration entries without an allowlist or sensitivity check, including credentials, tokens, or internal endpoints if present in the loaded configuration. This creates an overbroad privileged interface and exposes internal configuration data to the browser-side test context.

title: Cypress task permits arbitrary memory-field disclosure

The exact sensitivity of the configured memory fields is not visible in this file, so exploitability depends on the external configuration.

title: Path traversal in static-data file loader

A caller who can influence `file` can use traversal such as `../../config/secret` to read any accessible file whose final path ends in `.yml`, potentially exposing internal configuration or other sensitive data. The caller and attacker-facing route are outside this file, but the unsafe path construction and file-read sink are present here.

title: Unbounded chat input and streamed response buffering
description: The chat client accepts an arbitrarily large messages array and forwards it directly to the LLM-backed `/rest/chat` endpoint without any client-side size, count, or content-length bound. It also accumulates every streamed response chunk in an unbounded `chunks` array until yielded. The raw `feedback.comment` value is passed directly to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, creating a trusted HTML value without sanitization. This is the DOM HTML trust-boundary sink for attacker-controlled stored content.

title: Unbounded client-side loading of administration collections
description: Both administration list methods retrieve the complete user and feedback collections in one operation and only attach an Angular Material paginator after all records have already been received and stored in memory. The paginator therefore provides client-side display paging, not server-side result bounding. If these endpoints can return large collections, an authenticated administrator or any caller able to reach the component can trigger excessive response size, browser memory use, and rendering work.

trace.description: During component initialization, the component unconditionally starts full user and feedback collection loads; the service implementations and API callers are outside this file.
`userService.find()` and `feedbackService.find()` are collection requests with no page, offset, or server-side limit supplied by this component.
The complete user collection is assigned, iterated, and retained in memory, and `users.length` is recorded only after the full response has arrived.
The complete feedback collection is likewise assigned, iterated, and retained, with `feedbacks.length` calculated only after retrieval.

title: Authentication bypass via presence-only localStorage token check
description: LoginGuard treats the mere presence of any value in browser-controlled localStorage as proof that the user is authenticated. An attacker can set `localStorage.token` to an arbitrary nonempty string and pass this guard without token parsing, signature verification, expiration validation, or any server-backed authentication check. This permits unauthorized navigation to routes protected only by this client-side guard and may expose protected client functionality or data fetched without independent server authorization.

trace.description: The guard receives attacker-controlled browser storage state; the caller and token-writing code are outside this file. It checks only whether `localStorage.getItem('token')` returns a truthy value.
No token is parsed, cryptographically verified, checked for expiration, or validated against an authenticated session before the guard makes its decision.
The guard returns `true` solely because an arbitrary nonempty localStorage value exists, allowing the attacker to access any route protected only by this guard.

title: Client-side privilege escalation from unverified JWT role claims
description: AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, and DeluxeGuard authorize users by decoding JWT payload claims in the browser with `jwtDecode`. Decoding reads claims but does not verify the JWT signature, issuer, audience, or expiration. An attacker who can replace the localStorage token can construct a token whose payload contains `data.role: roles.admin` (or another privileged role), causing the guard to grant privileged client-side access. Any server-side privileged operation must independently enforce authorization; this guard is not a trustworthy authorization boundary.

trace.description: The guard obtains the token from attacker-controlled browser localStorage; the caller and token storage code are outside this file.
The token is passed to `jwtDecode`, which only parses the JWT payload. No signature, algorithm, issuer, audience, or expiration verification is performed in this file.
The decoded payload is used as the identity and authorization context for the admin guard, with the role taken directly from the unverified `data.role` claim.
A forged payload containing the expected admin role makes the guard return `true`; the analogous accounting and deluxe checks use the same unverified-claim design at lines 69-70 and 84-86.

title: Password-change credentials transmitted in a GET URL
description: The password-change flow sends the current password, new password, and confirmation password as query-string parameters on a GET request. URL values can be retained in browser history, intermediary/server access logs, monitoring systems, and Referer headers, exposing credentials and enabling replay if the URL is captured. The test explicitly validates this behavior rather than requiring a POST body or another protected credential-transfer mechanism.

trace.description: The test calls the password-change service with caller-supplied current, new, and repeat password values; the production caller is outside this file.
The expected request URL includes all three password values as plaintext query parameters: current=foo, new=bar, and repeat=bar.

The test asserts that the password-change operation uses HTTP GET, causing the credential-bearing URL to be sent as the request target and making it eligible for URL-based logging, caching, history, and leakage.

title: OAuth access token exposed in request URL
description: The OAuth login flow places a caller-provided OAuth access token in the URL query string when requesting Google user information. Bearer tokens in URLs are exposed to browser history, proxy/server logs, monitoring, and potentially Referer headers. The test directly asserts the access_token query parameter, indicating that the service's request construction uses this leakage-prone transport.

trace.description: The test supplies an OAuth access token to oauthLogin; the production caller and token source are outside this file.
The token is propagated into the Google user-info URL as the access_token query parameter.
The test confirms that the token-bearing URL is used for a GET request to the external OAuth API.

title: Sensitive account and payment routes lack authentication guards
description: Several authenticated account and transaction views are routable without LoginGuard. In particular, saved payment methods, order completion, order history, payment, and wallet can be reached directly by an unauthenticated browser session. This bypasses the application's client-side navigation control and exposes sensitive UI flows unless every component independently enforces authentication. A user can request routes such as /saved-payment-methods, /order-history, or /wallet directly instead of navigating through an authenticated flow. Server-side authorization may reduce the impact, but this routing file establishes no authentication gate for these sensitive views.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint is an Angular route handled by the caller outside this file; the router accepts direct navigation to the saved-payment-methods path.
The order history and order completion routes are also defined without canActivate, allowing direct navigation to transaction-related screens.
Payment and wallet routes likewise have no LoginGuard, so unauthenticated route navigation reaches sensitive payment/account components.

title: Account security and data-export route subtree is unguarded
description: The privacy-security route, which contains password change, two-factor authentication, data export, and last-login-IP functionality, has no LoginGuard or other route-level authorization check. Its children inherit no guard from the parent. An unauthenticated caller can directly navigate to paths such as /privacy-security/change-password or /privacy-security/data-export and instantiate these components. If the components do not independently enforce authentication, this permits access to account-security operations and personal data export; even if backend checks exist, the route configuration fails to provide the expected client-side access boundary.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint is an Angular route handled by the caller outside this file; the privacy-security parent route is registered without LoginGuard.
The parent defines child routes, but no guard is attached at the parent or child level, so the children are reachable by direct URL navigation.
The data-export operation is exposed as a child route without an authentication or authorization guard; change-password, 2FA, and last-login-IP are similarly unguarded siblings.

title: Two-factor authentication workflow entry is directly reachable
description: The two-factor authentication entry screen is directly routable without a guard or an explicit prerequisite-state check in the routing configuration. This permits callers to jump straight to /2fa/enter rather than following the preceding authentication workflow. If the component relies on routing state or client-side sequencing to determine that primary credentials were already verified, direct navigation can bypass the intended workflow and may enable MFA-flow abuse. Enforcement may exist inside the component or backend, so the finding is limited to the missing route-level control visible here.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint is the Angular route handled by the caller outside this file; the router registers the 2FA entry path as a standalone route.
The route has no canActivate guard and does not declare any prerequisite authentication or verification state.
TwoFactorAuthEnterComponent is instantiated for direct navigation, allowing the MFA workflow to be entered out of sequence unless it performs its own independent server-backed prerequisite check.

title: Unbounded challenge-solved notifications enable client-side resource exhaustion
description: The socket event handler accepts externally supplied “challenge solved” messages and invokes notification rendering for every message without any upper bound, eviction policy, rate limiting, or deduplication. Each accepted message is appended to the live `notifications` array and triggers change detection, allowing an attacker who can cause or spoof repeated socket events to grow client-side memory and DOM work indefinitely. This can degrade or exhaust the browser and may freeze the victim's session.

trace.description: The component receives `data` from the Socket.IO `challenge solved` event; the event source and its caller are outside this file.
For every event containing a truthy `data.challenge`, the handler invokes `showNotification(data)` without rate limiting, message-count limits, or deduplication.
The externally supplied challenge data is passed into `showNotification`, where its fields are used to construct a notification object.
Each event pushes another notification into the unbounded `notifications` array and then calls `detectChanges()`, causing unbounded retained objects and repeated UI rendering work.

title: Repeated socket events trigger unbounded progress requests
description: Every non-restore socket notification causes a separate `continueCode()` request. The handler has no batching, debounce, rate limit, or in-flight request guard. Repeated challenge-solved events can therefore create an unbounded number of backend requests and subscriptions, consuming client and server resources even when the resulting progress update is redundant.

trace.description: The component receives attacker-influenced or otherwise externally generated `data` from the Socket.IO `challenge solved` event; the event producer is outside this file.
For each qualifying event, the handler calls `saveProgress()` whenever `data.isRestore` is false, with no throttling or request coalescing.
`saveProgress()` invokes `challengeService.continueCode()` for every event and creates a new subscription, without an application-level rate or concurrency limit.
The service call is the resource-consuming network/backend operation that can be multiplied by repeated socket messages.

title: Client-side authentication relies only on attacker-controlled token presence
description: The checkout flow treats the mere presence of a browser-controlled `localStorage` value as proof that the user is authenticated. An attacker can set `localStorage.token` to any arbitrary string and cause this component to navigate directly to `/address/select`, bypassing the login redirect. This is not a valid authentication check because the token is neither parsed nor cryptographically verified here. The impact is limited if the address and payment APIs independently validate the token, but this component provides no trustworthy client-side authentication boundary.

trace.description: `checkout()` is the attacker-reachable component action; its caller and the surrounding route enforcement are outside this file.
The authentication decision checks only whether the browser-controlled `localStorage.token` key is non-null. No signature, expiry, issuer, or server-side session validation is performed.
When any value is present, the component navigates to the protected-looking address-selection flow without establishing that the token represents an authenticated user.

title: Client-supplied basket total is persisted as potentially authoritative state
description: The component accepts a basket total from an external child-component callback and writes it directly to browser `sessionStorage` as `itemTotal`, without validation or server-side rederivation. Browser storage is fully mutable by the user, so an attacker can alter this value before a later checkout/payment step. If downstream purchase logic treats `itemTotal` as authoritative, the attacker can submit an underreported total and potentially reduce the amount charged. That downstream use is outside this file, so exploitability and impact cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: `getBonusPoints(total)` receives the basket total from a caller outside this file, including the child purchase-basket component. The value is treated as trusted input.
The first tuple element, representing the item total, is converted to a string and stored without bounds checking, integrity protection, or recomputation from server-side basket data.

title: Password-change failures are logged only to the browser console
description: The password-change failure path is verified to emit the error through the browser's `console.log` rather than a security-aware, centralized, or structured logging mechanism. Failed password-change attempts are security-relevant events, and browser-console logging is not reliably available for incident detection or alerting and may be visible to the end user through developer tools. The test's explicit stubbing and expectation demonstrate this behavior, although the production implementation is outside this file.

trace.description: The mocked password-change service is configured to fail with an error; the service implementation and any caller beyond this test are outside this file.
The component receives the failed password-change result when `changePassword()` is invoked.

The test replaces `console.log` with a spy and requires it to be called with the failure string, establishing that the failure is handled via browser-console logging rather than an observable security-monitoring channel.

title: Privileged password policy is advisory and client-controlled
description: The privileged-account password policy check is advisory rather than an enforcement control. When the browser's localStorage email matches `support@.*`, the component only writes a console message if the new password is weak, then continues into `userService.changePassword` with the password unchanged. Because localStorage is client-controlled, an attacker can also alter or remove the email value to bypass the conditional entirely. If the backend relies on this client-side policy, a privileged account can be assigned a password that violates the intended corporate requirements, subverting the password-change workflow.

trace.description: The caller invokes the password-change workflow; the caller is outside this file. The component receives the current and new password values through its form controls.
The privileged-account determination is based on the browser-controlled localStorage `email` value, and the weak-password check is only performed for matching support accounts.
A failed privileged-password policy check only emits `console.error`; execution is not stopped and no validation error is set.

The component proceeds to the password-change service with the supplied password regardless of whether the privileged policy check failed. Any enforcement must therefore come from the external service/backend; if it trusts this client-side check, the workflow can be completed with a weak privileged password.

title: Raw password-change errors are logged to the browser console
description: Password-change failures are written to the browser console as an unredacted error object. Depending on the HTTP client's error contents, this can expose backend error messages, stack details, request metadata, or other security-relevant information to anyone with access to the browser session and makes sensitive failure data difficult to control or redact centrally. The component also provides no structured security-event record for failed password changes, limiting incident investigation.

trace.description: The external password-change service invokes the subscription's error callback when the operation fails; the service and its response contents are outside this file.
The received error object is propagated directly to a console logging call without filtering, redaction, or structured security-event handling.
`console.log(error)` exposes the raw password-change failure details in the browser console and does not create an auditable record of the failed security-sensitive operation.

title: Unbounded chat input, conversation history, and streamed LLM output
description: The component accepts arbitrary message content and appends it to the in-memory conversation without any length or conversation-size limit. It then sends the entire accumulated history to the chat backend. A caller outside this file can invoke `sendMessage` with a very large string, or repeatedly build a long conversation, causing large request bodies, excessive prompt-token consumption, client memory growth, and potentially expensive backend/LLM processing. The streamed assistant response is also concatenated indefinitely without a maximum response size.

trace.description: `sendMessage(content)` is the attacker-facing entrypoint in this file; its caller and any input constraints are outside this file. The method accepts arbitrary caller-supplied message content and only rejects empty content or a concurrent load.
The supplied content is appended directly to the local message array with no maximum message length, message-count limit, or total conversation-size limit.
The component derives `apiMessages` from the entire accumulated conversation, filtering only error messages; it does not truncate history or enforce a token/byte budget.
The unbounded conversation history is passed to `chatService.streamMessages`, creating an expensive LLM request whose prompt size and resulting cost can grow with every message.
Every streamed response chunk is appended to the assistant message without a maximum response length or stream timeout, allowing unbounded output and additional memory/token consumption.

title: Sensitive chatbot messages exposed through URL query parameters
description: The message received from the chat welcome screen is placed directly into the `initialMessage` query parameter when navigating to the conversation route. Chat messages may contain credentials, personal information, or other confidential content; embedding them in the URL exposes them to browser history, bookmarks, screenshots, referrer propagation, and URL/request telemetry. A user who later gains access to browser history or intermediary URL logs can recover the message. The workflow should pass the message through protected application state or a request body rather than placing it in a URL.

trace.description: `onMessageSent` receives the chat message from the child component; the caller and event source are outside this file.
The received message is propagated as the `initialMessage` query parameter during navigation.
The router constructs a conversation URL containing the full caller-provided message, making it available to URL history, referrers, and URL/request logging infrastructure.

title: Irreversible conversation deletion lacks confirmation or recovery control
description: The component performs irreversible deletion of all stored conversations without any confirmation, re-authentication, undo mechanism, or other compensating control. A user who activates the bound action can immediately erase the complete local conversation history, and an attacker able to induce or automate the UI action (for example through a compromised session or UI redress) can cause permanent data loss. The same design is also present for individual conversation deletion.

trace.description: The component exposes the conversation-management actions to its template; the caller/UI event binding is outside this file.
The handler invokes the storage service's bulk deletion operation immediately, with no confirmation, authorization check, or recovery path.
The in-memory conversation list is then cleared, leaving the user with no local indication or built-in way to restore the deleted history.

title: Raw backend error payload exposed as challenge content
description: When retrieving a coding-challenge snippet fails, the component substitutes the raw server error payload (`err.error`) as a `CodeSnippet` at line 53 and later exposes it through the public `snippet` property. The component template is therefore positioned to render backend error content directly to the user. If the API returns stack traces, filesystem paths, diagnostic data, or other internal details in error responses, an attacker can trigger the failing request (for example by supplying an invalid or unavailable `challengeKey`) and obtain those details through the challenge page. The component should use a controlled generic error state rather than treating arbitrary error responses as valid snippet content; confirmation of the exact exposure depends on the unseen template and backend error format.

trace.description: The component receives the route parameter `challengeKey`; the caller and route configuration are outside this file.
The route-controlled key is passed to the snippet service, and on failure the raw `err.error` response is cast to the expected snippet type instead of being replaced with a controlled error value.
The raw error-derived object is assigned to the public `snippet` property, which is consumed by the page template and can expose internal diagnostic content to the requesting user.

title: Continuation bearer code stored without cookie security attributes
description: The helper stores the server-issued continuation code in a client-managed cookie with only a one-year expiration. No Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite restrictions are configured. Because the value is a continuation/bearer code, an attacker able to obtain it through client-side script execution, browser extensions, or transport over an HTTP connection can reuse it for the challenge continuation workflow. The long lifetime increases the replay window. HttpOnly may not be available through this client-side cookie library, but the missing transport and cross-site protections are visible in this file.

trace.description: The exported helper receives the verdict and challenge-service/cookie-service dependencies from a caller outside this file; the helper is therefore the entrypoint for the continuation workflow in this file.
When the caller-provided verdict is true, the helper requests a continuation code from the challenge service and accepts the returned value after only checking that it is non-empty.

The continuation code is written to a browser cookie with a one-year expiration and no Secure, SameSite, or other security attributes, leaving the bearer value exposed to weaker cookie handling and client-side access.

title: Unrestricted repeated challenge-verification requests
description: The component exposes a callable `checkFix()` handler that immediately issues a backend verification request, with no debounce, in-flight request guard, cooldown, or client-side submission limit. A caller outside this file (the component template/user interaction) can invoke the handler repeatedly before prior responses return, generating an unbounded number of verification requests and potentially consuming backend CPU, connections, and rate-limit capacity. Server-side throttling is not visible here.

trace.description: The component's `checkFix()` handler is an attacker-triggerable UI entrypoint; its caller is outside this source file and can invoke it repeatedly through the rendered component.

Each invocation directly calls `codeFixesService.check(...)` using the current challenge key and fix index. There is no request-in-progress check, debounce, cooldown, or attempt counter before the request is started.
The service call is the resource-consuming sink: repeated invocations can create an unbounded stream of backend verification requests until an external control intervenes.

title: Unbounded challenge fixes and code rendered in the browser
description: The component accepts an unbounded array of fixes from an external caller and performs a randomizing sort over the entire array. It also later renders the selected fix and original snippet in CodeMirror without a size cap. If challenge data can be influenced by an attacker or an excessively large response is served, a single component initialization can force O(n log n) sorting and large editor-state/highlighting allocations, degrading or freezing the browser. No array, string, or rendering size limit is enforced in this file.

trace.description: The component receives the externally supplied `fixes` array through a required input; the caller is outside this file and no maximum number of fixes or maximum source length is declared here.
Initialization copies every supplied fix into an array of objects and sorts the complete collection using a comparator, with no size or complexity bound.
The unbounded collection reaches the randomizing `sort`, which performs attacker-amplifiable CPU and memory work for a single component initialization.

title: Bearer token exposed through localStorage
description: The component places the bearer authentication token in browser localStorage and then reads it into the uploader's Authorization configuration. Because localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the application's origin, an XSS or compromised third-party script can extract the token and replay it against authenticated APIs, including the file-upload endpoint. The component provides no indication of a safer HttpOnly-cookie-based session mechanism for this token.

trace.description: The Angular framework constructs this component from an external caller; during field initialization, the component creates a FileUploader for authenticated uploads.
The uploader's destination is configured as the application file-upload endpoint.

The bearer token is read directly from JavaScript-accessible localStorage and embedded into the uploader's authToken configuration, making it available to any script running in the origin and usable for authenticated request replay.

title: Client-controlled user ID enables feedback impersonation
description: The component obtains the authenticated user's ID, stores it in a client-side form control, and later copies that client-controlled value into the feedback object submitted to the backend. Because `userIdControl` is public and client-side state can be modified before `save()` executes, an attacker can substitute another user's ID and submit feedback attributed to that user. This is exploitable if the feedback API trusts the submitted `UserId` instead of deriving the identity from the authenticated session and enforcing ownership server-side.

trace.description: The component receives the current identity from `UserService.whoAmI`; the service response and its caller are outside this file.
The returned ID is copied into the public `userIdControl` and into the feedback object. The control is client-side state and is not protected by any authorization mechanism.
During submission, the component takes the value from the client-side control and assigns it to the sensitive `UserId` property without re-deriving or verifying it against the authenticated session.

The feedback object containing the caller-controlled `UserId` is sent to the backend through `FeedbackService.save`; the API must reject or ignore this property and derive the author identity server-side, otherwise an attacker can submit feedback as another user.

title: Unbounded system-wide notification polling interval can create request floods
description: The component accepts the configured polling interval without enforcing a positive, bounded value. Configuration data received from outside this file is used directly in `interval(pollFrequencySeconds * 1000)`, and the resulting observable immediately starts polling. A malicious or compromised configuration source, or an accidental extremely small value, can cause every client displaying this component to generate a high-rate request stream against the notification endpoint, creating client-side resource exhaustion and potentially a distributed request flood. The component should enforce a reasonable minimum and maximum polling interval before constructing the timer.

trace.description: The caller/configuration provider is outside this file; the component receives application configuration asynchronously and extracts the externally supplied notification URL and polling frequency.
The configured values are only checked for truthiness. There is no type, range, minimum, or maximum validation for `pollFrequencySeconds`; negative or arbitrarily small positive values are accepted.

The unchecked value controls the polling timer. With a very small interval, each browser repeatedly invokes the notification fetch path, and the `startWith(0)` call also performs an immediate request.

title: Unthrottled repeated challenge validation requests
description: The component exposes a repeatable challenge-check operation with no client-side throttling, in-flight request guard, or submission lock. `checkLines()` directly invokes the validation service every time it is called, including while a prior request may still be pending and without checking whether the challenge has already been solved. Because the caller can invoke this method repeatedly (and the backend route is outside this file), an attacker can automate requests to the challenge-validation endpoint and consume server CPU, network connections, and request capacity. This is a low-severity application-layer resource-consumption weakness unless stronger rate limiting exists in the service or infrastructure.

trace.description: The caller of `checkLines()` is outside this file; this public component method can be triggered repeatedly by the UI or by code invoking the component.
Each invocation immediately uses the current selected line collection and challenge key, with no rate-limit check, debounce, pending-request guard, or solved-state guard.

`VulnLinesService.check(...)` is the request sink for challenge validation. Repeated calls can generate an unbounded number of backend validation requests; any server-side or infrastructure rate limiting is not visible in this file.

title: Unsanitized export data written into a new browser document
description: The export response's `userData` is written directly into a newly opened document with `document.write`, without Angular sanitization or any HTML sanitizer. If exported data contains attacker-controlled fields (for example, a stored profile value or other persisted user content), an attacker can place HTML/script payloads in that data and cause it to execute when another user opens the export result. The API call and response originate outside this file, but this component provides the unsafe client-side rendering sink.

trace.description: The component invokes the data-export service; the service implementation and attacker-facing API entrypoint are outside this file, so the response contents cannot be trusted here.
The API response's `userData` field is copied into component state without validation or sanitization.

The value is inserted as raw HTML into a new window using `document.write`. HTML elements, script-capable markup, or event-handler attributes contained in attacker-influenced export data can execute in the new document.

title: External CAPTCHA HTML trusted without sanitization
description: The CAPTCHA response field `data.image` is passed to Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's HTML sanitization. The value comes from an external service response and is then presumably rendered by the component template. If the CAPTCHA endpoint, response path, or image content can be influenced by an attacker, malicious SVG/HTML markup can execute in the application origin. The source and template binding are outside the visible code, so exploitability depends on whether the service response is attacker-controllable; the unsafe trust decision is directly present here.

trace.description: The component receives CAPTCHA data from `ImageCaptchaService`; the service's network entrypoint is outside this file.
The response's `image` field is assigned to component state with no validation or sanitization.

`bypassSecurityTrustHtml` marks the externally supplied value as trusted HTML, disabling Angular's normal sanitization before the template renders it. Attacker-controlled SVG/HTML content could execute in the application context.

title: Client-controlled address identifier reaches address lookup without a visible ownership check
description: The component uses the caller-controlled `sessionStorage` value `addressId` directly as the identifier for an address lookup. Any user able to modify browser storage can substitute another address ID. This file performs no ownership or authorization check before requesting the address, so exploitation depends on whether `AddressService.getById` and its backend endpoint enforce per-user ownership. If they do not, User A can replace `addressId` with User B's ID and retrieve or use User B's address during checkout.

trace.description: `ngOnInit` receives attacker-modifiable browser state from `sessionStorage`; the caller and storage contents are outside this file.
The value is passed unchanged as the target resource identifier to `AddressService.getById`.

The address lookup is initiated without any local check that the selected address belongs to the authenticated user. A crafted `addressId` can therefore cause an IDOR/BOLA request if the service/backend does not independently authorize it.

title: Checkout workflow trusts an arbitrary client-controlled delivery method ID
description: `selectMethod` accepts an arbitrary method ID and `chooseDeliveryMethod` writes it to `sessionStorage` before navigating to payment. The component does not verify that the ID is one of the methods returned by `DeliveryService.get()`, that a method is actually selected, or that the method's price and properties are server-derived. A user can invoke the handler or edit storage to submit an arbitrary delivery-method ID, potentially selecting an unauthorized or cheaper method if downstream checkout logic trusts this client-controlled state. The server must re-derive the method and price and authorize it for the order.

trace.description: `selectMethod(id)` is an externally triggered component handler; its caller is outside this file and can supply an arbitrary ID.
The supplied ID is assigned directly to `deliveryMethodId` without checking membership in the fetched `methods` list or validating its server-side state.

The unchecked value is persisted in browser storage and the payment workflow is entered immediately. Client-controlled delivery selection must not be trusted for authorization, pricing, or fulfillment decisions.

title: Unredacted configuration errors exposed in browser console
description: The configuration request's error callback writes the entire error object to the browser console. Because the object originates outside this file, it may contain backend response details, stack traces, request metadata, or other sensitive fields; any such data becomes directly visible to the user through browser developer tools. The file provides no redaction or production guard around this diagnostic output. The exact sensitivity of the returned error object cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The component receives the configuration observable result, including errors generated by the external configuration service.
The externally supplied error is passed unchanged to the error callback.
The complete error object is emitted with console.log, exposing any sensitive fields or diagnostic details it contains to the browser user.

title: Unverified JWT claim reaches an Angular HTML security bypass
description: The component reads the JWT from attacker-modifiable browser localStorage, decodes the payload without verifying its signature, and inserts the payload's lastLoginIp into HTML via DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(). If the component template binds lastLoginIp with an HTML-rendering binding such as [innerHTML], a payload such as can execute in the application's origin. The explicit trust bypass disables Angular's normal sanitization, and no validation or sanitization is applied before the value reaches the sink.

trace.description: ngOnInit is the component entrypoint; the caller/framework invokes it outside this file and it begins processing authentication-derived data.

The component retrieves the authentication token from localStorage and decodes it with jwtDecode. jwtDecode only parses the token and does not verify its signature, so the payload is not trustworthy from this component's perspective.
The unverified payload is parsed and its data.lastLoginIp claim is selected for display without validation or sanitization.

The attacker-influenced claim is interpolated into an HTML string and explicitly marked trusted with bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), disabling Angular's HTML sanitization. Any template HTML-rendering binding of lastLoginIp can therefore execute injected markup or event-handler payloads.

title: Unauthenticated password-recovery flow enables account enumeration and unrestricted attempts
description: The password-recovery flow exposes account existence and the account's security question to an unauthenticated user-supplied email address. The component sends the email directly to the security-question lookup service, then visibly distinguishes a matching account (question returned and reset controls enabled) from a non-matching account (controls disabled). An attacker can automate this flow to enumerate registered email addresses and obtain security-question prompts, reducing the work required to guess recovery answers. The lookup and reset operations also have no rate-limiting control in this component, so repeated unauthenticated attempts can be generated against the recovery workflow; any server-side throttling is not evident here.

trace.description: The component receives attacker-controlled email input through the public password-recovery form; the caller/template event wiring is outside this file. The email control only applies required/email format validation, which does not prevent probing valid and invalid accounts.

After a one-second UI delay, the value of the email control is passed directly to the unauthenticated security-question lookup service. The debounce only delays browser events and is not an endpoint-level abuse control.

The response is used to distinguish whether an account exists: a returned question enables the security-question and password controls, while no question disables them. This observable difference exposes account-registration status and the security-question prompt.

The component submits email, security answer, and new password to the password-reset service without any visible attempt throttling, lockout, or other abuse control. Repeated callers can therefore drive password-recovery attempts; server-side controls cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: NFT mint eligibility enforced only by a client-side button state
description: The component treats the NFT eligibility state as a client-side UI control rather than enforcing it in the mint workflow. `checkNftMinted()` only sets `mintButtonDisabled` and `challengeSolved`, but `mintNFT()` checks only `session` and proceeds to approve 1000 BEE and call `mintNFT()`. A caller who invokes the component method directly or otherwise bypasses the disabled button can execute the mint flow without the challenge being solved or without confirming that the wallet has not already minted. The smart contract must independently enforce these conditions; this component does not.

trace.description: The component receives the externally controlled wallet/session state and initializes the NFT workflow. The caller and wallet interaction are outside this file.
The component obtains the signer and prepares an approval for 1000 BEE, but there is no check of `challengeSolved`, `mintButtonDisabled`, or an equivalent server-authorized eligibility token.
The only eligibility result obtained from the backend is used to disable the UI button; it is not enforced by `mintNFT()` itself.

After the approval, the component invokes the NFT contract mint operation. If the contract does not independently enforce one-mint and challenge requirements, this operation can be repeated or performed without solving the challenge.

title: Ethereum chain-change listeners are registered without cleanup
description: Every component initialization registers a `chainChanged` listener on `window.ethereum`, but the component never removes it when destroyed. Navigating away and back can leave callbacks from destroyed component instances registered. A subsequent chain change invokes every accumulated handler, causing repeated authentication, wallet connection/disconnection, balance RPC calls, change detection, and potentially repeated wallet prompts. This creates a client-side resource and event-amplification leak.

Each initialization attaches another bound handler to the global provider. No corresponding `removeListener`/`off` call or component-destruction cleanup exists in this file.
A chain-change event invokes `handleChainChanged()`, which starts authentication again and can trigger disconnect/connect and balance-fetch operations for every leaked component listener.

title: Unbounded withdrawal amount reaches the faucet contract
description: `withdrawAmount` is populated from component/UI state and is passed directly to the faucet contract without checking that it is a finite, positive, bounded amount. The only guard is whether a wallet session exists. A caller can supply null, zero, negative, fractional, or excessively large values, causing failed transactions and gas consumption; if the faucet contract does not impose its own strict bounds, the same path can permit withdrawals beyond the intended faucet amount. Client-side amount validation is absent and cannot be relied on as the contract's authorization or economic control.

The function checks only `session` and performs no numeric, positivity, maximum, or precision validation on `amount` before proceeding.

The unvalidated amount is passed directly into the signer-backed faucet contract's withdrawal operation, allowing repeated malformed or oversized transaction attempts and relying entirely on unseen contract logic for economic limits.

title: Authentication and temporary 2FA tokens are stored in localStorage
description: The test explicitly verifies that a returned authentication token is persisted in browser localStorage and that a temporary TOTP token is also persisted there. Web Storage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the origin, so an XSS or compromised third-party script can extract these bearer credentials and use them to impersonate the user or complete the 2FA flow. The production assignment is not shown in this spec, but the test codifies and confirms the component's insecure token-storage behavior.

The component's login workflow is invoked with that response, exercising the production token-handling path.
The test asserts that the returned authentication token is available through localStorage, establishing that the component stores the bearer token in script-readable Web Storage.
A failed login response containing a temporary TOTP token is supplied to the component, exercising the MFA continuation path.
The test asserts that the temporary TOTP token is stored as localStorage key totp_tmp_token before navigation to the 2FA page, making the MFA credential accessible to any same-origin script.

title: Login redirect target is accepted from a query parameter without visible validation
description: The login flow takes a redirectUrl value from the route query parameters and passes it directly to navigateByUrl without an allowlist or same-origin validation visible in this file. If an attacker can cause a victim to visit a login URL containing a crafted redirectUrl, the post-login navigation target may be abused for phishing or workflow redirection. The test uses only '/profile', so whether Angular or the component applies additional validation is unconfirmable from this file.

The component login flow is executed while the caller-controlled redirect target is present in the route snapshot.
The test verifies that the supplied query-parameter value is passed directly to router.navigateByUrl, with no allowlist or same-origin check asserted in this file.

title: Hardcoded testing credentials exposed in the frontend bundle
description: The login component ships a plaintext testing username and password in the frontend source. These values are compiled into the client bundle and can be discovered by any user, allowing attackers to attempt authentication with the testing account wherever it remains enabled. The password is also a reusable credential rather than a protected secret.

The component declares a public testing username directly in client-side source code.

title: Bearer authentication token stored in script-readable client storage
description: After a successful authentication response, the bearer token is persisted in localStorage. Any script executing in the application's origin, including a script introduced through an XSS or compromised dependency, can read this token and use it to impersonate the user. The same path also stores the token in a client-managed cookie without an explicit Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite configuration.

The component receives the authentication object, including its bearer token, from the login service response.

The same token is also written through a client-side cookie API with only an expiration option; no Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite protections are explicitly configured, and client-side code cannot make the cookie HttpOnly.

title: TOTP temporary authentication token stored in localStorage
description: When authentication requires TOTP, the server-provided temporary token is stored in localStorage. This authentication artifact is therefore readable by any same-origin script and remains persisted beyond the current in-memory execution, creating a path to MFA-flow abuse if an attacker can execute JavaScript in the origin or otherwise access browser storage.

title: OAuth accounts use a predictable reversible email-derived password
description: The OAuth flow is explicitly expected to create or authenticate a regular account using a password derived solely from the user's email: the email is reversed and Base64-encoded (`bW9jLnRzZXRAdHNldA==`). Base64 is reversible encoding, and the derivation is deterministic, so anyone who knows an OAuth user's email can reproduce the password and potentially authenticate through the regular login path. The subsequent test also confirms that the same predictable password is used to log in when account creation fails, making the derived credential a persistent authentication mechanism rather than a one-time exchange. The implementation that performs the derivation is outside this file, but this test directly codifies the insecure behavior as the expected contract.

The component processes the OAuth result, and the test expects the OAuth flow to continue into regular account creation.

The expected account-creation request contains a password equal to a reversed email encoded with Base64, demonstrating a deterministic and reversible authentication secret. Base64 does not provide password hashing or secrecy.

title: OAuth fallback authenticates with the predictable derived credential
description: When account creation fails because the account already exists, the flow is expected to log in using the same deterministic email-derived password and an OAuth bypass indicator. This means knowledge of the user's email is sufficient to reconstruct the credential used by the regular login operation, and the fallback path preserves the weakness for existing accounts.

The component's initialization handles the failed creation path and proceeds to the regular login operation.

title: Private key is transmitted to the application backend
description: The component collects a value explicitly named `privateKey` and transmits it to the application service for every form submission. If this is a wallet or signing private key, the design gives the server—and any intermediary, diagnostic instrumentation, or compromised API handling this request—custody of a credential that should normally remain client-side. An attacker who compromises the backend or its request/error logging could obtain the key and use it to sign transactions or control the associated assets. The component also performs no local protection such as preventing repeated submissions, although server-side controls cannot be confirmed from this file.

`KeysService.submitKey` is the sink that sends the private key to the backend. This creates server-side custody of the sensitive signing credential and exposes it to backend compromise or insecure request/error handling.

title: Client-side accounting authorization trusts decoded token role
description: The component determines whether the accounting UI is available by decoding a token and trusting the client-visible `role` claim. The token is sourced from browser-side authentication state (the component uses `localStorage` for the token), and no server-side authorization check is present in this code path. An attacker who can replace or forge the client-side token payload with `data.role = accounting` can make `isAccounting()` return true and potentially expose accounting-only navigation or controls. This is a client-side authorization/trust-boundary flaw; the impact depends on whether the corresponding backend operations independently enforce the accounting role.

The component obtains a decoded authentication token using `tokenDecode()`. Elsewhere in this same component, authentication state is read from browser-controlled `localStorage`, so this is a client-side token trust boundary rather than a server-enforced authorization decision.

The decoded, client-supplied `payload.data.role` value is directly compared with the accounting role and returned as the privilege decision. There is no ownership, server-side role verification, or signature-verification check visible between decoding and this decision.

description: The component accepts an order identifier directly from the client-controlled route and passes it to the order lookup service without any visible ownership or authorization check. The returned order data is then rendered, and its address identifier is used to retrieve a related address. If the backend service does not independently enforce that the authenticated user owns the order, User A can replace the route `id` with User B's order ID and view the order and address information.

The order-derived address ID is used in a second lookup, and the resulting address is stored for rendering without a visible check tying it to the current user or authorized order.

No client-side maximum, pagination, or other bound is applied. Whether an attacker can create or obtain such an order is not determinable from this file.

title: OAuth accounts receive predictable, reversible passwords
description: The OAuth flow derives the user's local password deterministically from the email address by reversing it and Base64-encoding it. Base64 is reversible encoding, not password protection, and the resulting password is sent to the account-save operation and then reused for ordinary login. Anyone who knows an OAuth user's email can compute the same password; if the account is provisioned or an existing account falls through the save error path, the attacker can authenticate through the password login flow without possessing the OAuth identity. The client also controls the password-generation logic, so this must not be treated as a secret or authentication factor.

That predictable value is submitted as both password and passwordRepeat to the account-save operation, with no server-verifiable secret or random credential generated in this component.
If account saving fails, the flow intentionally proceeds to login anyway, preserving the assumption that the derived password is a valid credential.
The same deterministic value is sent to the ordinary login endpoint with oauth: true, creating an authentication path that can be reproduced by anyone who knows the user's email.

title: Bearer token stored in weakly protected browser storage
description: The component stores the bearer authentication token in a client-readable cookie without explicitly enabling Secure or SameSite protections, and also duplicates it in localStorage. Any script executing in the origin can read the localStorage token and the non-HttpOnly cookie; if the application is ever served over plaintext HTTP, the cookie may also be transmitted without the Secure restriction. Theft of either bearer token permits session impersonation until expiration or invalidation.

The successful login callback receives authentication.token and authentication.bid from the authentication response.

The same bearer token is stored in localStorage, which is readable by any JavaScript executing under the application origin and therefore directly exposes the session to script-level token theft.

title: Raw API errors are logged directly to the browser console
description: The test explicitly requires the component to write raw API errors directly to the browser console. Because browser-console output is visible to the end user and the underlying error may contain backend or operational details, this can expose implementation information and provides no structured, centralized security logging or redaction. The production logging call is implemented outside this spec file, so the finding is based on the behavior this test requires from OrderSummaryComponent.

A user can modify deliveryMethodId, addressId, or paymentId in DevTools before this component initializes, causing the client to request another user's address, payment record, or delivery method. The component performs no ownership or authorization check; whether the backend independently enforces authorization is not visible in this file. title: Checkout trusts client-controlled resource identifiers
description: placeOrder constructs the checkout request using paymentId, addressId, and deliveryMethodId taken directly from mutable sessionStorage. A caller can alter these values before invoking the externally triggered placeOrder handler, potentially causing an order to use another user's address or payment method, or to reference resources the current user is not authorized to use. No ownership verification or server-derived resource binding is present in this component. The backend may mitigate this, but that control cannot be established from this file.

title: Unbounded order-history materialization can exhaust client resources
description: The component requests the complete order history with no visible pagination, maximum-result parameter, client-side cap, or incremental loading. The returned collection is reversed and every order and nested product is copied into new objects; each order also creates a separate MatTableDataSource. If the backing order-history endpoint permits a large history, an authenticated user or attacker repeatedly triggering this view can force the browser and potentially the API response path to allocate and process an unbounded number of orders and products, causing excessive memory and CPU consumption or client-side denial of service.

The response is iterated in full, and every order's complete product list is copied into a new in-memory array. There is no pagination, truncation, or maximum-count check before processing.
For every returned order, the component retains the copied data and allocates a separate MatTableDataSource, multiplying memory usage with the number of orders and products.

title: String-valued controls bypass MIME validation
description: The exported MIME validator immediately accepts any string-valued control without examining or validating the string. An attacker who can submit a string instead of a File can therefore bypass this client-side MIME check entirely. If the upload workflow relies on this validator as its enforcement point, a caller can submit arbitrary URL/path or other string content and evade the intended image-type restriction; server-side validation is required to prevent direct-request bypasses.

The validator branches solely on whether the control value is a string. No validation of the string's content, URL, extension, or associated file occurs.
Every string value is returned as valid via of(null), bypassing the magic-byte checks applied to File values. A caller can therefore pass an arbitrary string and receive no validation error.

title: Payment-card deletion relies entirely on downstream authorization
description: The component accepts an arbitrary payment-card identifier in `delete(id)` and forwards it directly to the payment service without any client-side ownership or authorization check. If the backing delete API does not independently scope the identifier to the authenticated user, an attacker can substitute another user's card ID and delete that card. The component should not be treated as an authorization boundary, but this code provides no compensating check before issuing the destructive request.

The caller-supplied identifier is passed unchanged to `paymentService.del(id)`. No ownership, user association, or authorization decision is made in this component.
The payment-service delete operation is the destructive sink. Any authorization failure in the backing API would allow deletion of a card belonging to another account.

title: Unsanitized payment-service errors logged to the browser console
description: The component writes complete error objects to the browser console for payment-card loading and deletion failures. Those objects are supplied by the payment service and may contain backend exception details, request metadata, or other sensitive payment-related information. Browser-console logging is visible to anyone with access to the session and can unnecessarily expose diagnostic or sensitive data; errors should be sanitized before logging, or security-relevant failures should be sent through controlled application logging.

title: Client-controlled wallet payment amount reaches balance mutation
description: The wallet payment flow treats a client-controlled session-storage value as the payment amount and sends it to the wallet update service. `walletTotal` can be modified by the user before this component runs, including setting a negative or otherwise manipulated amount. The client-side balance check is also based on the same attacker-influenced `totalPrice`. If the server accepts the submitted balance/amount without independently deriving the purchase total from the basket and authoritative pricing, an attacker can underpay, bypass insufficient-balance checks, or potentially increase wallet funds by submitting a negative amount. The server-side validation is not visible in this file, but the client-controlled value reaches a financial mutation directly.

The attacker-influenced amount is submitted in the wallet mutation request as `{ balance: this.totalPrice, paymentId: this.paymentId }`; no authoritative basket total or server-derived amount is established in this file before the financial operation.

Because the error originates from an external configuration request, it may contain backend URLs, response bodies, stack traces, or other internal diagnostic details. Any user who can trigger this failure can inspect the browser console, exposing implementation details that can assist reconnaissance. The file does not sanitize or restrict the logged error.

A caller can modify the client-side request or invoke the service directly with a different author, allowing reviews to be attributed to another user unless the server ignores and re-derives this field.
