The item identifier reaches `basketService.del(id)`, allowing an attacker who can invoke the handler with another item's ID to attempt cross-user deletion. The related quantity path similarly calls `get(id)` and `put(id, ...)` at lines 172 and 176.

title: Guest basket permits zero and negative quantities
description: The guest-basket quantity path does not enforce a minimum quantity, unlike the authenticated path, which clamps the value to at least 1. Calling `dec()` when a guest item has quantity 1 stores quantity 0, and repeated calls can store negative quantities. The component then uses that quantity in total and bonus calculations. If guest basket contents are later submitted or transferred for checkout without server-side normalization, an attacker can create zero/negative line items and potentially obtain an incorrect or negative total.

trace.description: The component exposes `dec(id)` as a guest-reachable quantity-decrease entrypoint; its caller/template is outside this file.
For unauthenticated users, `addToQuantity()` finds the local guest item and computes `existingGuestItem.quantity + value` without enforcing a lower bound or rejecting negative results.
The unchecked quantity is written back to the guest basket. A decrement from 1 writes 0, and further decrements write negative values.
The unchecked quantity is subsequently multiplied into the displayed item total and bonus calculation, demonstrating that the invalid state affects business calculations.

title: Client-controlled identity and unrestricted recycle object submitted to API
description: The recycle submission is built as a mutable, client-controlled object and sent wholesale to the recycle API. The component assigns `UserId` from the client-side `whoAmI()` response and accepts `addressId` from a child component without performing an ownership check. A caller who modifies the browser state or intercepts the request can substitute another user's `UserId` or `AddressId`; additionally, arbitrary enumerable properties added to `recycle` can be serialized and submitted. If the API binds request properties directly to the Recycle model, this enables unauthorized association with another user's address and mass assignment of server-controlled fields.

trace.description: The component's `save()` method is invoked by the caller/template outside this file; it accepts no trusted server-side identity or authorization context.
The component places the current user's ID into a mutable object on the client, rather than having the server derive the owner from the authenticated session.

The address identifier is received from the child address component through `getMessage(id)` and stored without an ownership check. The quantity and pickup fields are also copied into the same mutable object; the controls are only client-side validation.

The entire mutable `recycle` object is passed to the service. There is no explicit allow-list, removal of caller-controlled identity fields, or per-resource authorization check before the POST request.

title: Recycle quantity constraints are enforced only in the client UI
description: The component can submit values without checking form validity at the submission boundary. Although `recycleQuantityControl` has client-side minimum and maximum validators, `save()` directly reads its value and sends it to the API. Client-side validators can be bypassed by invoking the method, modifying the control, or issuing the request directly. If the server relies on these UI constraints, an attacker can submit quantities outside the intended 10–1000 range, potentially causing invalid or abusive recycling records.

trace.description: The `save()` method is callable from the component's external template/caller; this file does not establish a server-enforced validation boundary.
The quantity control declares minimum and maximum validators, but these validators exist only in the Angular client and are not themselves a security control against direct API callers.

`save()` reads the control value and submits it without checking `valid` or revalidating the range. A direct invocation or modified request can therefore bypass the intended quantity bounds if the API does not independently enforce them.

title: Unbounded loading of recycle records
description: On initialization, the component requests all recycle records and stores the complete response without pagination, a client-side limit, or incremental loading. If the corresponding API returns an unbounded or very large collection, an unauthenticated or low-privilege caller able to reach this page can cause excessive response transfer and browser memory consumption with repeated requests.

trace.description: `ngOnInit()` is invoked by Angular's framework lifecycle outside this file and initiates the recycle-record retrieval.
`findAll()` calls the recycle service to retrieve the collection and assigns the complete result to `this.recycles`; no page, limit, cursor, or client-side cap is supplied.
The service request is the outbound API sink for the unbounded collection operation. The response is accepted wholesale rather than bounded before storage/rendering.

title: Weak minimum password length in registration flow
description: The registration form accepts passwords as short as five characters. The control is client-side validation only and can be bypassed by directly invoking the registration API, so unless the server independently enforces a stronger policy, an attacker can create accounts protected by low-entropy passwords that are more susceptible to guessing and credential stuffing. The maximum length of 40 also unnecessarily limits passphrases, although the minimum-length weakness is the security issue established here.

trace.description: Caller-controlled registration input is received through the password form control; the caller and template are outside this file. The control permits passwords meeting only the required and minimum-length validators.
The accepted password value is copied into the user registration object without any stronger local policy or indication that a server-side password-strength requirement is enforced.
The password is submitted to the user registration service, allowing passwords of five characters to reach account creation if the API does not independently reject them.

title: Unsanitized challenge descriptions rendered through Angular HTML security bypass
description: The component explicitly disables Angular's built-in HTML sanitization for each challenge description. Challenge data is received from the API and the description is copied directly into `bypassSecurityTrustHtml()` without an application-controlled allowlist or sanitizer. If a challenge description contains attacker-controlled markup, the corresponding template HTML binding will trust and render it, allowing stored client-side XSS such as injected event-handler attributes or malicious elements to execute in users' browsers.

trace.description: The callback receives challenge records from `challengeService.find()` and other external service responses; the caller and API endpoint are outside this file.

Each API-provided challenge is transformed while preserving `challenge.description` as `originalDescription`; no validation or sanitization is applied to the description before the HTML rendering value is created.

The raw challenge description is passed to `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml()`, explicitly marking attacker-influenced HTML as trusted and bypassing Angular's normal XSS protections. When consumed by the component template's HTML binding, payloads such as event-handler markup can execute in the browser.

title: URL search parameter is marked as trusted HTML
description: The component explicitly disables Angular's HTML sanitization for the search query taken directly from the URL. An attacker can send a victim a link containing a malicious `q` parameter; the value is assigned to `searchValue` as trusted HTML and is consequently eligible for HTML insertion by the component template. This permits reflected client-side XSS payloads such as an HTML element with an event-handler payload, subject to the template's binding context.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; `filterTable` receives the current URL query parameter through Angular's `ActivatedRoute` and reads attacker-controllable `q`.
The query value is trimmed and used as the component's search state without HTML sanitization. It remains attacker-controlled while being stored for display.

The attacker-controlled query string is passed to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's contextual HTML sanitization before it is rendered through the component's HTML display binding.

title: API product descriptions bypass Angular HTML sanitization
description: Product descriptions returned by `ProductService.search` are copied from the API response and then explicitly marked as safe HTML. This bypasses Angular sanitization for content that is not proven to be trusted in this file. If an attacker can create or influence a product description, the resulting markup can execute as stored client-side XSS whenever the description is rendered by the product table or `ProductComponent`.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; `ngAfterViewInit` receives product records from `ProductService.search`, including each product's externally supplied `description` field.
The returned product array is passed directly to `trustProductDescription` before being used to populate the table and product display data.

Each API-provided description is passed to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, disabling Angular's sanitization and allowing attacker-controlled HTML or event-handler markup to reach the component's HTML rendering path.

title: Raw progress-restoration errors exposed through client-side console logging
description: The component logs the raw error object from the progress-restoration request directly to the browser console. Because the error originates from an external service response, it may contain backend response bodies, stack traces, identifiers, or other internal diagnostic details. Any user able to open developer tools can inspect these values, and the logging is not redacted or restricted to a safe error category. This also weakens incident handling because the failure is only emitted as an unstructured client-side console message rather than being sent through a controlled, security-aware logging path.

trace.description: The externally generated Socket.IO `server started` event invokes this callback; the event source and caller are outside this file.
The callback reads client-controlled continuation-code cookies and uses them to initiate progress restoration through the challenge service.
A failed restoration request supplies its externally generated error object to the error handler without sanitization or classification.
The complete error object is written to the browser console, exposing any backend details included in the error to the end user and any scripts or extensions with console access.

title: Raw configuration errors exposed in the browser console
description: The component logs the raw error object from the application-configuration request directly to the browser console. If the service or backend includes stack traces, request metadata, internal URLs, or other sensitive diagnostic details in that error object, any user who can open developer tools can view them. The file provides no sanitization, redaction, or production-only diagnostic guard. This is a low-confidence, low-severity logging exposure because the exact contents of the error object are defined outside this file.

trace.description: Angular invokes the component lifecycle hook; the framework caller is outside this file.
The component subscribes to the externally supplied application-configuration request result, including its error path.
The unfiltered error object is written to the browser console, potentially exposing diagnostic or internal response details to anyone with client-side access.

title: Attacker-controlled order ID is explicitly trusted as HTML
description: The test explicitly supplies an HTML payload as the order ID and verifies that the component wraps it in a `<code>` element and passes it to `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml`. This indicates attacker-influenced order identifiers are treated as trusted HTML rather than rendered as text. If the production component binds this trusted value to the template, markup such as injected elements or event-handler payloads can reach the DOM without Angular sanitization. The external caller/source of `orderId` is outside this file; this test establishes that the component's intended behavior is to trust the value.

trace.description: The test injects an HTML-formatted order ID (`Link`); the real caller or external source of this value is outside this file.
The injected value is returned by the mocked tracking service as the order response and then processed by `ngOnInit`.

The test asserts that the component passes the interpolated order ID to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, confirming that the dynamic value is deliberately marked as trusted HTML instead of being safely rendered as text.

title: Attacker-controlled order ID marked as trusted HTML
description: The component explicitly disables Angular's HTML sanitization for an order identifier received from the tracking API. An attacker who can influence the stored orderId (for example through order-related input) can cause HTML markup to be constructed inside the trusted value; when the component template renders orderNo as HTML, payloads such as closing the code element followed by an event-bearing element can execute in the user's browser. No sanitization or allow-listing is applied before bypassSecurityTrustHtml().

trace.description: The component receives the asynchronous tracking-service response. The service and its caller are outside this file, so the response data must be treated as externally influenced input.
The response's orderId field is interpolated directly into an HTML string, with no validation or sanitization of the value.

DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() marks the interpolated attacker-influenced HTML as safe, bypassing Angular's normal HTML sanitization. When the resulting trusted value is bound by the component template, injected HTML and event-handler payloads can execute in the browser.

title: Bearer authentication token stored in script-accessible storage and an unsecured cookie
description: After successful MFA verification, the component stores the bearer authentication token in both `localStorage` and a JavaScript-managed cookie. `localStorage` is readable by any script executing in the origin, and the cookie is created without `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, or `SameSite` attributes. Consequently, an XSS payload can directly retrieve the token, while any accidental HTTP deployment can transmit the cookie over plaintext and the cookie remains accessible to client-side scripts. Theft of this token can allow an attacker to impersonate the authenticated user until the token expires or is revoked.

trace.description: The `verify()` handler receives the MFA token from the component form and invokes the authentication service. The user-facing caller and the service implementation are outside this file.
The user-supplied six-digit token is passed to `TwoFactorAuthService.verify()`, which returns an authentication object containing a bearer token.
The returned bearer token is persisted in `localStorage`, making it directly readable by JavaScript executing in the application's origin.

The same bearer token is written through the client-side cookie service with only an expiration option. No `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, or `SameSite` protection is specified; because JavaScript creates the cookie, it cannot be `HttpOnly`.

title: Accounting authorization is based on an untrusted client-side token claim
description: The component makes an accounting-role decision entirely from a decoded token payload: `loginGuard.tokenDecode()` is used to obtain `payload.data.role`, and the result is compared directly with the accounting role. No signature, expiration, or server-side authorization check is visible in this path. Because the token is read and controlled on the client, a user who can replace or forge the stored token can make the application treat them as an accounting user and expose accounting-only UI or route access. Any corresponding server operation must independently enforce the role; this component does not provide that control.

trace.description: The `isAccounting()` method is called by the component template or another caller outside this file to decide whether accounting functionality is available.
The method obtains a decoded token payload through `tokenDecode()`; this file shows no signature, expiration, or issuer verification at this point.

The client directly trusts `payload.data.role` to determine whether the caller has the accounting role. A modified local token can therefore influence this authorization decision and reveal or enable accounting UI/routes unless separately blocked server-side.

title: Authentication state is inferred from token presence alone
description: `isLoggedIn()` treats the mere presence of a value in browser `localStorage` under the `token` key as proof that the user is logged in. There is no validation of token structure, signature, expiration, or server session state in this method. If this method is used as a client-side access gate, an attacker can place any arbitrary value under `localStorage.token` and cause the application to enter its authenticated UI state. This is not evidence that backend APIs are bypassable, but it is an insecure client-side authentication design and must not be used as the authorization control for protected actions.

trace.description: The `isLoggedIn()` method is called by the component template or another caller outside this file as the client-side logged-in check.
The method returns the raw truthiness of `localStorage.getItem('token')`; any nonempty attacker-supplied value is accepted without token or session validation.

title: Raw API errors are exposed through client-console logging
description: The component writes the raw error object from the user-details API request directly to the browser console. Because the object is not sanitized or reduced to a generic error code, backend response bodies, request details, or stack-trace information included in the error may be exposed to anyone who can inspect the client console. This also provides unstructured diagnostic output rather than a controlled security logging path, weakening incident investigation and potentially disclosing internal implementation details.

trace.description: The component receives dialog data from its caller outside this file, establishing the context for the user-details operation.
During initialization, the externally supplied user identifier is used to request user data from UserService.
When the request fails, the complete error object is passed to console.log without redaction, filtering, or structured security logging.

title: Client-controlled wallet amount bypasses payment constraints
description: The wallet amount has client-side validators, but `continue()` does not check whether the form control is valid before persisting the value and entering the payment flow. A caller can invoke this method with an invalid, negative, oversized, non-numeric, or otherwise manipulated value; browser-side validators can also be bypassed through DevTools or direct `sessionStorage` modification. The resulting `walletTotal` is available to the subsequent payment page, so any downstream logic that treats it as authoritative can allow an attacker to bypass the intended wallet amount constraints or manipulate the credited/payment amount. The server must independently validate and derive the effective amount rather than trusting this client-controlled value.

trace.description: The Angular template or another caller outside this file can invoke the public `continue()` method; this method receives no validated amount argument and does not require the form to be valid.

The amount control declares only client-side Angular validators for required, minimum, and maximum values. These validators do not enforce constraints against direct method invocation or browser-side tampering.

`continue()` unconditionally writes `balanceControl.value` to `sessionStorage` without checking `balanceControl.valid`, normalizing the value, or obtaining server-side authorization. It then navigates into the payment workflow, where the stored value can be consumed as `walletTotal`.

title: Wallet address is sent as identity without proof of private-key ownership
description: The component treats the wallet address returned by the injected provider as an identity and sends it to the application through `walletAddressSend` without requesting or verifying a cryptographic signature. A wallet connection exposes an address, but does not by itself prove to the backend that the caller controls the corresponding private key. If the service uses this value to authorize minting, account linking, or other privileged wallet actions, an attacker can submit another user's address directly to the backend and impersonate that wallet. The server should issue a nonce and verify a signed challenge before accepting the address as authenticated identity.

trace.description: Angular invokes `ngOnInit` as a framework lifecycle entrypoint; the caller is outside this file and it starts the wallet authentication flow via `handleAuth()`.
`handleAuth()` obtains the connected account through `connect()` and assigns the provider-reported address to `metamaskAddress`. No nonce, message, or signature is requested or verified.
The unverified provider account is copied into `userData` and passed to the application service as the wallet identity.

`walletAddressSend(this.metamaskAddress)` sends the address to the backend, with no cryptographic proof accompanying it. This is the trust sink if the backend uses the request to authenticate or authorize wallet-specific behavior.

title: Remote Solidity compiler artifacts are not integrity-pinned
description: The component passes a remotely hosted Solidity compiler URL to `solidityCompiler` without any visible checksum, signature, or other artifact-integrity verification. The URL is selected from a local version map, but the JavaScript compiler artifact itself is still retrieved from `binaries.soliditylang.org` at runtime. If the hosting infrastructure, delivery path, or artifact is compromised, the browser may execute a tampered compiler and produce attacker-controlled bytecode or otherwise manipulate the compilation result before the connected wallet signs a deployment transaction.

trace.description: `compileAndFetchContracts` receives Solidity source from its caller outside this file; the caller can trigger compilation of source supplied through the sandbox editor.
The selected compiler version is converted into a remote URL under `https://binaries.soliditylang.org/bin/`; no digest, signature, or allow-listed artifact content is associated with the URL.
The remote compiler URL and caller-provided contract source are passed to `solidityCompiler`, which retrieves/uses the compiler artifact without an integrity check visible in this component.

title: Web3 chain-change listeners leak across component lifecycles
description: Each component initialization registers a `chainChanged` listener on `window.ethereum`, but component destruction only destroys the CodeMirror editor and never removes that listener. Repeated navigation/remounting accumulates references to destroyed components. A subsequent chain change invokes `handleAuth` once per stale instance, causing repeated wallet disconnect/connect operations and repeated chain-add requests. An attacker or automated client-side action that repeatedly mounts the component can therefore create unbounded listener growth and amplify wallet/provider activity, degrading the browser or causing wallet prompt/API flooding.

trace.description: The external wallet provider's `chainChanged` event is registered during component initialization; the provider retains the bound component handler.
`ngOnDestroy` destroys only `editorView`; there is no corresponding `window.ethereum.removeListener` call, so each destroyed component's chain-change listener remains registered.
Every stale listener reaches `handleAuth`, which performs provider connection work through `connect`, multiplying resource use and wallet/provider operations for a single chain-change event.

title: Frontend backend endpoint defaults to unencrypted HTTP
description: The exported frontend environment configuration hardcodes the backend origin as plain HTTP. If this development configuration is bundled or otherwise used in a deployed frontend because the documented file replacement is omitted or misconfigured, browser-to-backend traffic—including authentication material or other sensitive data—can be observed or modified by a network attacker. The `localhost` default also causes a deployed browser to contact a service on the user's machine, which could expose requests to an untrusted local service. The production replacement comments reduce certainty that this reaches production, but the unsafe transport default is present in the shipped configuration source.

The configuration explicitly marks this as non-production, making it intended for development, while relying on build-time replacement to prevent this object from being used in a deployed build.
The backend URL is configured with the unencrypted `http` scheme and a localhost host, so requests using this configuration do not receive transport confidentiality or integrity.

title: Plaintext account credentials exposed in client-side source
description: The exported challenge instruction embeds a usable email address and plaintext password in frontend source. Because this instruction is part of the client-side bundle, any unauthenticated user who downloads or inspects the application can recover the credentials and authenticate as the associated account. This is an authentication secret exposure and an unsafe deployment/configuration choice; the password should not be shipped to clients, even if the account is intended for testing.

trace.description: The caller outside this file consumes the exported `ExposedCredentialsInstruction` object and makes its hint content available as part of the frontend challenge flow.
The client-side instructions explicitly direct users to inspect `main.js` to find hardcoded credentials.
The expected login email is embedded in the frontend instruction and is supplied to the email field.
The expected plaintext password `IamUsedForTesting` is embedded in the frontend source and supplied to the password field, providing the credential exposure sink.

title: Plaintext user password embedded in frontend source
description: The client-side challenge instructions contain Bender's plaintext password (`OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!`) as a literal. Because this TypeScript module is bundled and delivered to the browser as part of the frontend challenge framework, users can inspect the source or bundle and recover the credential. If the value is valid outside the instructional helper, it enables direct authentication as Bender; even if intended only for challenge-state detection, embedding a real password in client code exposes a reusable authentication secret.

trace.description: The exported challenge instruction object is loaded by an external frontend challenge framework; that caller and the resulting browser delivery are outside this file.

The challenge configuration passes a plaintext password literal to `waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty` as the value that should not be entered, embedding the credential directly in client-side source.
The plaintext credential is present in the shipped frontend module and can be recovered by any user with browser or source-bundle access, creating a reusable authentication secret exposure.

title: Frontend source discloses weak administrator credentials
description: The exported frontend challenge instruction discloses the administrator's actual login identifier and progressively reveals the password `admin123` in client-shipped source. The instruction then directs the user to click the login button and explicitly confirms that this results in administrator access. Any user able to inspect the frontend bundle or follow the challenge can authenticate as the administrator, bypassing the intended privilege boundary. This is a hardcoded weak credential and an insecure authentication design; if this file is included in a deployed build, the credential is exposed to every client.

trace.description: The exported `PasswordStrengthInstruction` object is consumed by a caller outside this file, making the instruction content part of the client-facing application surface.
The instruction hardcodes the administrator email address and tells the user to enter it on the login page.
The instruction progressively accepts `admin`, `admin1`, `admin12`, and finally `admin123` as the administrator's password, exposing the weak credential directly in source code shipped to the client.
The workflow directs the user to submit the login form and explicitly states that the result is administrator authentication, making the disclosed credential an authentication sink.

title: Plaintext account password embedded in frontend source
description: The frontend challenge instruction embeds the plaintext value `ncc-1701` as a password-related literal. Because this file is part of the frontend, its source and compiled bundle are available to users, allowing anyone to recover the credential if it is still valid for Jim's account. The literal is passed to the input-validation helper rather than used to authenticate, but its presence discloses a likely real account password and creates a credential exposure risk.

trace.description: The exported `LoginJimInstruction` object is the frontend challenge entrypoint; its caller and eventual browser delivery are outside this file.
The login challenge explicitly references Jim's password while instructing the user to enter an incorrect password, indicating that the value is treated as a known credential.
The plaintext value `ncc-1701` is embedded in the frontend source as an argument to `waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty`, making it recoverable by inspecting the source or client bundle.

title: Admin access gate trusts an unverified client-side JWT role
description: The admin-login wait helper treats a client-side JWT payload as authoritative without verifying the token's signature, issuer, expiration, or other claims. An attacker who can modify the token in localStorage can provide a fabricated token whose decoded role is `admin`; this causes the helper to proceed through client-side admin-only workflow gates even though the token may not represent an authenticated administrator. Any privileged operation must perform independent server-side authorization rather than relying on this client-side check.

trace.description: The exported `waitForAdminLogIn` function receives control from a caller outside this file and implements the client-side gate for an administrator login state.

The function reads the token directly from attacker-modifiable browser localStorage and decodes it with `jwtDecode`; this operation parses claims but does not verify the JWT signature or validate expiration and issuer.

The decoded, unverified `payload.data.role` is compared against the literal `admin`, and the helper returns success when it matches. A forged localStorage token can therefore satisfy this client-side admin gate; no authentication or server-side authorization check occurs in this code path.

title: Unbounded recursive filesystem traversal and file reads
description: The exported `findFilesWithCodeChallenges` function accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied path list and recursively walks every reachable directory, enumerates every entry, and reads matching files in full. There is no recursion-depth limit, file-count limit, file-size limit, timeout, or cancellation mechanism. If this function is reachable from an attacker-influenced workflow, a path targeting a very large or deeply nested tree can consume excessive filesystem I/O, memory, and CPU and cause service degradation or an outage.

trace.description: `findFilesWithCodeChallenges` is exported and receives `paths` from its caller outside this file; the function performs no trust, scope, or resource-limit validation on those paths.
Each supplied path is inspected and directories are recursively traversed by reading all directory entries and invoking the same function for every child.
Recursive calls expand the traversal to arbitrarily deep and large directory trees, with no maximum depth or number of files.
Each non-directory file is read completely as UTF-8 and retained in the returned match object; there is no file-size or aggregate-memory cap.

title: Unescaped file-derived challenge keys enable regex injection and ReDoS
description: File contents determine `challengeKey`, which is interpolated directly into dynamically constructed regular expressions without escaping or an allow-list. A caller able to cause this function to process attacker-controlled files can supply regex metacharacters or complex quantified expressions in a challenge marker. Those expressions are compiled and evaluated against source content, allowing regex injection and potentially catastrophic backtracking/CPU exhaustion. The same unescaped key is also used in the line-marker regexes.

trace.description: The exported file-discovery function accepts paths from a caller outside this file, so the processed file set and potentially its contents may be externally influenced if the caller exposes this API to untrusted input.
Files selected through that path input are read into memory as raw source text.
Challenge keys are extracted directly from source text by splitting marker contents; no character allow-list or regex escaping is applied.

The unescaped `challengeKey` is interpolated into a string passed to `source.match`, which dynamically compiles and evaluates it as regular-expression syntax. Complex attacker-controlled patterns can alter matching behavior or trigger excessive backtracking.

title: Unescaped challenge name enables log injection
description: The exported lookup function accepts a caller-provided challenge name and incorporates it directly into a warning log message. If an attacker can cause a missing-name lookup using a value containing newlines or log-control characters, they can forge additional log entries or corrupt log parsing, reducing the reliability of security monitoring and incident investigation.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies the exported `challengeName` argument to `findChallengeByName`.
The supplied name is compared against cached challenge names; a value not present in the cache reaches the warning path without character validation or normalization.
The caller-controlled string is concatenated directly into a log message. Newline or control characters can make attacker-generated content appear as separate or misleading log records.

title: Challenge flags broadcast to every connected client
description: `sendNotification` constructs a notification containing the challenge flag and broadcasts it through the process-wide Socket.IO instance. The notification is not scoped to the user who solved the challenge or otherwise access-controlled, so all connected clients can receive the flag. This can disclose challenge secrets to other users and undermine the integrity of the challenge workflow.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies a `ChallengeModel` to the exported `sendNotification` function; the function does not establish a recipient or authorization context.
The function derives a flag from the challenge name and places that value into the notification object alongside challenge metadata.
The notification, including the `flag` field, is retained in the global notification structure without per-user access control.
When the Socket.IO instance is available, the complete notification is emitted globally rather than to the authorized solver only.

title: Unbounded notification cache growth
description: The module maintains an unbounded in-memory `notifications` array. Every eligible invocation appends a notification, including repeated calls for the same challenge; the duplicate check only suppresses some broadcasts and does not prevent the append. If an attacker can reach this exported utility through a caller, repeated requests can grow memory without a cap and make the duplicate scan increasingly expensive.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies a challenge to the exported `sendNotification` function; the function is callable without a visible invocation quota or rate control.
The function checks whether the challenge key has appeared before, but this check only controls whether the socket event is emitted and does not reject duplicate notifications.
Each eligible invocation unconditionally appends another notification to the process-global array, with no maximum length, expiration, or eviction policy.

title: Product configuration permits negative prices
description: Product prices are accepted as arbitrary numbers, including negative values, in both the complete application configuration and the deep-partial validation path. If an attacker can influence a product configuration through an exposed configuration or product-management path, a negative price can cause checkout totals or refunds to be credited rather than charged. The schema does not establish the required non-negative business invariant.

trace.description: A caller outside this file supplies application configuration that is parsed against the exported schemas.
The complete application configuration accepts an array of product objects without adding any additional price invariant.
The product schema defines price only as a generic number; negative values are valid under this schema.

title: OAuth authorized redirects accept unrestricted destinations
description: OAuth redirect configuration is validated only as an array of arbitrary strings. No URL scheme, host, or allowed-origin constraint is enforced for either the redirect URI or its optional proxy value. If this configuration is supplied or modified through an untrusted configuration-upload or management path, an attacker can introduce a redirect target controlled by the attacker, potentially turning the OAuth flow into an open redirect or redirect-token exposure. The downstream OAuth consumer is outside this file, so exploitability depends on how these values are used.

trace.description: A caller outside this file supplies a possibly incomplete YAML/application configuration for validation.
The application subsection is made deep-partial, allowing an external configuration fragment to replace or add the Google OAuth settings.
Each authorized redirect is accepted when uri and proxy are merely strings; the schema does not constrain them to approved HTTPS origins or otherwise prevent attacker-controlled destinations.

title: Logger format omits timestamp and correlation context
description: The exported application logger is configured with Winston's `simple()` format, which does not add a timestamp or request/correlation identifier to log records. As a result, security-relevant events logged through this logger may be difficult to correlate across requests or reconstruct into an incident timeline. This is a monitoring weakness; whether callers add their own context or the deployment platform adds timestamps cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: This module exports a singleton logger used by callers outside this file; those callers' security-relevant events enter the logging path through this initialization.
The logger sends messages to a console transport, with production-like environments accepting messages at the `info` level or higher.

title: Hardcoded private key enables JWT forgery

title: Role middleware accepts expired signed tokens
description: The accounting and deluxe authorization helpers verify only the token signature and then inspect decoded role claims. They do not validate expiration or other JWT temporal claims. title: Unsalted MD5 used for authentication-related hashing
description: The exported hash helper uses unsalted MD5. If used for passwords, reset secrets, or other authentication credentials—as is typical for a security utility—an attacker obtaining the hash database can use fast brute force and precomputed tables to recover values. MD5 provides neither salting nor password-specific work factor.

title: Coupons lack authenticity and can be forged
description: Coupon values are merely Z85-encoded and checked for a current-month format; there is no MAC or signature binding the discount to a trusted issuer. An attacker can encode a value such as the current month followed by an attacker-selected discount and have it accepted by discountFromCoupon. title: Substring-based redirect allowlist is bypassable
description: The redirect allowlist uses substring matching rather than exact URL comparison or origin-based validation. If the external caller redirects when this predicate returns true, this bypasses the intended allowlist and creates an open redirect.

title: Authentication identity is trusted from a spoofable request header
description: userEmailFrom returns the x-user-email request header without deriving the identity from a verified token or checking that the header matches the authenticated user. If a handler uses this helper for account lookup, authorization, or security-sensitive actions, an attacker can impersonate another email. title: Immutable-column protection is bypassable with validate:false
description: The `noUpdate` constraint is enforced only when Sequelize validation is enabled. title: Unbounded FTP-folder enumeration and deletion can consume startup resources
description: The cleanup routine enumerates every matching PDF under `ftp/` into an in-memory array and then removes each file sequentially, with no bound on the number of matched files or a time/resource limit. title: Unauthenticated clients can delete global websocket notifications
description: Any client that establishes a Socket.IO connection can receive every cached notification, including its `flag`, and then emit `notification received` with that flag. description: Custom application assets can be configured as arbitrary URLs. title: Dependency-checker failures cause an uncontrolled startup crash
description: The exported validator accepts a caller-supplied `packageDir` and invokes the dependency checker without ensuring that checker failures produce the same result shape as normal returns. title: Unvalidated caller-controlled URL enables server-side request forgery
description: The exported `downloadToFile` helper accepts a caller-supplied URL and passes it directly to the `download` library without validating the scheme, hostname, resolved address, or redirect destination. Any attacker-controlled caller that reaches this helper can cause the server to make requests to internal services such as localhost, private-network hosts, or cloud metadata endpoints, potentially disclosing the response through the subsequent file write or enabling internal-service interaction.

title: Unbounded JSON parsing permits resource-exhaustion denial of service
description: The exported JSON parser processes the entire caller-provided string with no input-size, nesting-depth, token-count, or execution-time limit. If an attacker-facing route passes unbounded request data to this helper, a large or highly complex JSON document can consume substantial CPU and memory while building the parser state and result array, causing denial of service.

description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/memories endpoint retrieves every memory record in one database operation and eagerly includes the associated UserModel. There is no pagination, limit, filtering, or other request-level bound. As the number of memories grows, an attacker can repeatedly request this endpoint to force unbounded database reads, object materialization, serialization, and response transmission, degrading availability or exhausting application/database resources.

The handler performs an unrestricted findAll over the entire MemoryModel table and eagerly loads associated UserModel records. No limit, offset, cursor, or filter is applied.
All materialized records are serialized into a single JSON response, allowing the attacker to consume database, application memory, CPU, and bandwidth proportional to the full dataset.

title: Caller-controlled UserId is persisted as memory ownership
description: The POST /rest/memories handler persists the caller-supplied req.body.UserId as the memory's ownership/association field. The handler itself does not derive or verify this identifier from the authenticated user and passes it directly into MemoryModel.create. If the upstream appendUserId middleware only fills the field when absent, or can otherwise be bypassed, an authenticated attacker can submit another user's ID and create a memory attributed to that user. The middleware is outside this file, so the exact overwrite behavior cannot be confirmed here.

The handler copies the request body UserId field into the record without deriving it from a trusted authenticated identity or explicitly rejecting caller-supplied ownership fields.

MemoryModel.create persists the caller-influenced UserId association. Supplying another user's identifier can create a record owned by or attributed to that user unless the external middleware unconditionally overwrites the field.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of internal application metrics
description: The unauthenticated GET /metrics route exposes the Prometheus registry directly. The registry contains aggregate operational and business-sensitive metrics, including total wallet balance, registered-user counts, order/review/feedback/complaint counts, and cheat-score information. Because the handler performs no authentication or authorization check before returning the registry, an external caller can retrieve internal application telemetry and infer business activity and user-related information.

The metrics registry includes user and wallet gauges, including total registered users and the total balance of all users' digital wallets.
The update loop populates the registry with order, review, user, wallet, feedback, and complaint counts, as well as challenge and cheating-related metrics.
The handler serializes and returns the complete Prometheus registry to the requester, with no filtering or authorization boundary.

title: Unauthenticated metrics endpoint lacks rate limiting
description: The public metrics handler has no request-rate, concurrency, or caching control. Each request invokes register.metrics(), which serializes the complete in-process registry, including default and application metrics. An attacker can repeatedly request /metrics to consume application CPU and response bandwidth; the risk is increased because the route is unauthenticated and the handler itself provides no throttling.

Every request proceeds directly to Prometheus registry serialization rather than using a bounded or cached response.
register.metrics() serializes the full metrics registry and writes it to the response, allowing repeated unauthenticated requests to consume CPU and network resources.

title: Unbounded retrieval and in-memory reversal of all orders
description: The accounting order-list endpoint retrieves the entire orders collection without pagination or a result limit, then reverses the full result set in application memory. As the collection grows, an authenticated accounting user can repeatedly invoke GET /rest/order-history/orders to force unbounded database reads, memory allocation, and CPU work, potentially degrading service or causing process exhaustion. The route is accounting-protected, which reduces exposure but does not bound the resource cost of each request.

The handler issues an unbounded collection read with no limit, skip/offset, cursor, or pagination parameters.
The complete result is reversed in application memory and returned in the response, causing the endpoint to materialize and process the entire order collection for every request.

title: Unauthenticated access to premium content
description: The premium-content route is reachable without authentication or authorization and unconditionally serves an asset located under a `private` directory. The route name suggests access should depend on payment or another entitlement, but neither payment verification nor any user authorization check occurs. An attacker can request the published route directly—without sending 1 BTC—and receive the premium wallpaper. The path's obscurity is not an access-control mechanism.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: the application registers `servePremiumContent()` for `GET /this/page/is/hidden/behind/an/incredibly/high/paywall/that/could/only/be/unlocked/by/sending/1btc/to/us` with no authentication middleware.
The exported handler receives the request and proceeds directly to the response without checking authentication, payment status, entitlement, or any other authorization condition.
The handler unconditionally sends the supposedly private premium wallpaper to any caller who reaches the route.

title: Unauthenticated checkout of arbitrary baskets (BOLA)
description: The exported checkout handler is registered as unauthenticated and accepts a basket identifier from the URL. It loads the basket solely by that identifier, without checking that the basket belongs to the authenticated user or that the caller is authenticated. The handler then consumes the basket contents, removes its items, and returns an order confirmation. An attacker can submit another user's basket ID to place or destroy that user's order and obtain order-related data.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is reached by POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout with no authentication middleware, and receives the attacker-controlled basket ID in req.params.id.

The handler reads req.params.id and queries BasketModel by only that ID. No authenticated-user or ownership predicate is included in the lookup, and the authenticated customer, if any, is used only to derive an email for the PDF.

After processing, the handler updates the selected basket and destroys all BasketItem records for the supplied basket ID, then returns an order confirmation. Thus an attacker who substitutes another user's basket ID can trigger the checkout mutation against that basket.

title: Caller-controlled UserId enables unauthorized wallet debit and credit
description: The checkout endpoint allows the caller to choose req.body.UserId and uses it directly as the target for wallet debiting and bonus-crediting. Because the route is unauthenticated and no relationship is established between UserId and the basket owner or authenticated principal, an attacker can target another user's wallet for payment or credit arbitrary users with bonus points. The wallet balance check and mutations therefore operate on an attacker-selected account.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout is registered without authentication middleware, and the handler receives arbitrary request-body properties including UserId.

The handler branches on req.body.UserId and uses that caller-supplied value to find a wallet. If paymentId is wallet, it checks and debits the wallet belonging to that UserId; it does not derive the user from a trusted session or verify ownership of the basket.
The same caller-selected UserId is used to increment the wallet balance by totalPoints. There is no authorization check tying the target wallet to the caller or to the basket being checked out.

title: Forgery and indefinite replay of campaign discounts
description: The campaign coupon mechanism treats base64 as if it provided coupon authenticity. The caller supplies couponData, which is decoded into a coupon code and timestamp; a discount is accepted when the values match one of several hardcoded historical campaign records. There is no signature/MAC, server-issued redemption token, current-date expiry check, or single-use tracking. Anyone can construct the base64 representation of a historical campaign such as WMNSDY2019 with its known timestamp and repeatedly obtain the 75% discount.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the checkout handler accepts the request body and passes it into calculateApplicableDiscount during order total calculation.

When the basket has no applicable stored coupon, the function accepts req.body.couponData, decodes it with base64, and uses the resulting caller-controlled code and date as the discount decision inputs. Base64 decoding provides no authenticity or integrity protection.

A discount is granted solely when the decoded values equal a hardcoded campaign's code and validOn timestamp. The historical timestamp is not compared with the current date and no redemption state is recorded, so a known token can be replayed indefinitely.

title: Non-atomic checkout permits duplicate orders and financial mutations
description: Checkout performs multiple externally observable and financially relevant mutations without an atomic transaction or idempotency control. Concurrent requests for the same basket can both load it before BasketItem deletion, each decrement inventory, debit or credit wallets, insert an order, and only later delete the basket items. An attacker can race duplicate checkout requests to create duplicate orders, multiply bonus credits, and cause inconsistent inventory or wallet state.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the checkout route accepts repeated requests for the same basket identifier and has no visible idempotency key or concurrency guard.
The basket and its products are read before any lock or transactional boundary is established. Multiple concurrent handlers can therefore observe the same basket contents.

Each handler independently decrements inventory and performs wallet mutations before deleting basket items, and then inserts an order. These operations are not enclosed in one transaction and the cleanup occurs only after PDF generation, allowing concurrent requests to duplicate the order and associated mutations.

title: Payment method access is not audit logged
description: Authenticated payment-card access is not recorded in this handler. The GET endpoint retrieves a user's stored payment methods and returns card-related metadata (including the last four digits), but there is no audit log for the access. An attacker who obtains or abuses an authenticated session could repeatedly access payment metadata without producing an application-level audit trail, impairing detection and incident investigation.

The handler queries all payment cards associated with the UserId placed on the request body and prepares card metadata for the response.
The handler returns the payment-method data, including masked card numbers, without emitting any security-relevant audit event or access log.

title: Payment method deletion is not audit logged
description: Deletion of a stored payment method is a security- and business-relevant event, but this route performs the destructive operation and returns success without recording who deleted which card, when it occurred, or whether the attempt failed. This prevents reliable detection and reconstruction of unauthorized payment-method deletion.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an attacker-facing HTTP request through its caller outside this file; the route is DELETE /api/Cards/:id and is protected by security.appendUserId().
The card identifier comes from req.params.id and the user scope comes from req.body.UserId; the handler attempts to destroy the matching record.
The handler reports successful deletion without writing an audit log for the destructive payment-method operation.

title: NFT verification accepts an unproven wallet address as ownership proof
description: The unauthenticated walletNFTVerify handler treats a caller-supplied wallet address as proof that the caller owns the wallet or minted the NFT. The listener records only that an address appeared as an NFT minter; it does not establish possession of the corresponding private key, require a signed challenge, or bind the event to an authenticated user. Because Ethereum addresses are public, an attacker can observe a minted address and submit it in walletAddress to receive the successful challenge response. The first attacker to submit the address also deletes it, preventing the legitimate user from using it.

trace.description: POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify reaches the exported handler without authentication middleware; the route caller is outside this file.
The handler receives walletAddress directly from the request body and uses it as the claimed wallet identity, with no signature, nonce, authentication identity, or ownership check.
The address is compared against the process-global set populated from public NFTMinted events. Membership proves only that the address appeared as a minter, not that the current caller controls it.

A matching caller-controlled address is accepted as a successful challenge solution and removed from the set, allowing an observer to solve the challenge and potentially front-run the legitimate wallet owner.

title: Unbounded in-memory storage of NFT minter addresses
description: The NFT event listener stores every distinct minter address in an unbounded in-memory Set. Entries are removed only when a verification request happens to consume the address; there is no maximum size, expiration, eviction, or backpressure. If the monitored contract can be induced to emit many NFTMinted events from distinct addresses, the process retains attacker-influenced state indefinitely and can eventually suffer memory exhaustion. The attack requires generating the corresponding blockchain events, so the practical exploitability and cost depend on the contract's mint controls.

trace.description: GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen invokes the exported listener handler without authentication middleware; the route caller is outside this file.
The persistent contract listener processes each NFTMinted event and receives the minter address from the external blockchain event stream.
Each previously unseen minter address is retained in the process-global addressesMinted collection.
The Set grows without a size limit or expiration as addressesMinted.add stores attacker-influenced unique values; cleanup occurs only if a separate verification request consumes an exact address.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of asset from private directory
description: The unauthenticated route returns a file located under a directory explicitly named `private`. Any caller can request the route and receive `frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/thank-you.jpg`; there is no authentication or authorization check in this handler. If the `private` asset is intended for internal or restricted use, this exposes it publicly. The sensitivity of the image and whether deployment-level controls restrict the route cannot be confirmed from this file.

The handler does not inspect the request identity or enforce any role or ownership check before serving the file.

title: Unauthenticated in-memory image processing enables upload resource exhaustion
description: The profile-image upload route is reachable without authentication middleware and accepts the uploaded file into memory before performing any authentication check. `uploadToMemory.single('file')` runs before this handler, and the handler then reads `req.file.buffer` and passes the entire buffer to `fileType.fromBuffer()` before checking whether the requester has a valid token. Because no request/file size limit or rate limit is visible in this file, an unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly submit large multipart uploads, causing memory consumption during buffering and additional CPU consumption during file-type detection. Any infrastructure-level upload limit would reduce or eliminate the impact, but no such control is shown here.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: POST /profile/image/file invokes the exported `profileImageFileUpload()` handler after `uploadToMemory.single('file')`, `ensureFileIsPassed`, and metrics middleware, with no authentication middleware declared for the route.

The entire unauthenticated buffer is parsed by `fileType.fromBuffer(buffer)`, which consumes attacker-controlled memory/CPU; the token lookup occurs only afterward at line 35. Repeated large requests can therefore exhaust resources before the access check rejects them.

title: Platform-dependent path traversal in quarantine file serving
description: The handler uses a caller-controlled `params.file` value to construct the path passed to `res.sendFile`. Its validation rejects only forward slashes, but `path.resolve` uses platform-specific separators. On Windows, an attacker can supply a value such as `..\..\config\secret.json`; it contains no `/`, passes line 13, and resolves outside `ftp/quarantine/`. The handler then serves the resulting arbitrary file. This can expose configuration, credentials, source, or other internal files. The caller and route registration are outside this file, so reachability and authentication middleware cannot be confirmed here.

The handler receives the attacker-controlled route parameter `params.file` and assigns it directly to `file`.
The only validation checks for the forward-slash character. It does not reject backslash separators or verify that the resolved path remains within the quarantine directory.
The unchecked value is resolved into a filesystem path and served. On Windows, backslash traversal such as `..\..\path\to\secret` can escape `ftp/quarantine/` and disclose arbitrary readable files.

title: Unauthenticated access to arbitrary recycle records
description: The unauthenticated GET /api/Recycles/:id route invokes this exported handler (the caller and route registration are outside this file). The handler takes the caller-controlled path parameter `req.params.id`, parses it, and queries `RecycleModel` solely by that identifier. A requester can substitute another user's recycle ID and obtain that record, constituting unauthenticated BOLA/IDOR. Because `findAll` is used and the parsed value is not restricted to a scalar ID, JSON array input may also broaden the lookup to multiple IDs depending on ORM behavior.

The path parameter `req.params.id` is parsed and used as the sole lookup criterion. No user identity, ownership field, or role check is added to the query.
All records matching the attacker-selected identifier are serialized and sent to the requester without an authorization check.

title: Unauthenticated triggering of repeat notifications for solved challenges
description: The GET /rest/repeat-notification route is registered without authentication or authorization. The handler accepts an attacker-controlled challenge name, resolves the corresponding challenge, and invokes sendNotification whenever that challenge is marked solved. Thus an unauthenticated caller can trigger notifications for solved challenges without proving that they are the relevant user or otherwise authorized to repeat the notification. An attacker can repeatedly submit another challenge's name to cause unauthorized notification side effects and potentially disrupt or spam users.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler receives an Express Request for GET /rest/repeat-notification; the caller and route registration are outside this file, and the route is declared with no authentication middleware.

The supplied challenge name is used to resolve a challenge record.
For any resolved challenge whose solved flag is true, the handler performs the notification side effect without an ownership, identity, or role check.

title: Authenticated server-side request forgery via profile image URL
description: The authenticated profile-image URL endpoint accepts `req.body.imageUrl` and passes it directly to `fetch()` without restricting the scheme, hostname, resolved IP, redirects, or private-network destinations. An authenticated attacker can submit URLs targeting loopback services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other internal hosts, causing the server to make requests from its network position. The response is then written to the application filesystem, and errors are silently converted into storing the attacker-controlled URL as the profile image.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled HTTP request; its caller and route registration are outside this file. The route is POST `/profile/image/url` and is registered without route-level authentication middleware.
The handler reads `req.body.imageUrl` and assigns it to `url` without a domain, scheme, or private-address allow-list.

The attacker-controlled URL is used as the destination of an outbound server-side request. The only preceding check is whether the supplied token maps to a logged-in user, which does not constrain the destination.
The response from the attacker-selected destination is consumed and persisted by the server, confirming that the request is operational rather than merely validated.

title: Unbounded remote image download can exhaust server resources
description: The same endpoint streams the complete response from an attacker-selected URL into a file under the application's public image directory. There is no response-size limit, `Content-Length` enforcement, download timeout, rate limit visible in this handler, or quota/count control. An authenticated attacker can host or target a response that never ends or is extremely large, causing persistent disk consumption and tying up request/file-stream resources until service degradation or exhaustion.

trace.description: The exported handler receives attacker-controlled profile-image upload requests; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The route is POST `/profile/image/url`.
The attacker supplies the remote URL through `req.body.imageUrl`; no size, timeout, or download policy is applied to this input.
The handler performs an outbound fetch and accepts any successful response body without checking a maximum response size or imposing a timeout.

The entire response stream is piped to a write stream in the application's filesystem and awaited to completion. A large or non-terminating response can consume disk space and hold server resources indefinitely.

title: Unthrottled security-answer password reset enables account takeover by brute force
description: The unauthenticated password-reset endpoint accepts an email address and security-question answer, performs the answer check, and changes the account password without any rate-limiting, attempt counter, lockout, CAPTCHA, or other abuse control visible in this handler. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for a target user's security answer and, after a successful guess, take over the account by setting a new password. A global limiter may exist outside this file, but no compensating control is present in the shown reset flow.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: the exported handler is registered as unauthenticated POST /rest/user/reset-password and receives attacker-controlled request data through the Express Request parameter.
The handler accepts the target email, security-question answer, and replacement password directly from the request body.
The supplied email is used to locate the security answer associated with a user, with no attempt tracking or throttling in this flow.
The caller-controlled answer is checked against the stored answer, and a successful guess immediately permits the password mutation.
After the answer check succeeds, the handler updates the identified user's password, completing the account-reset operation without an abuse-control check.

title: Password reset attempts and successful resets are not audited in the handler
description: A successful password reset is a security-relevant account event, but this handler performs the password mutation and returns success without recording an audit event containing at least the target account, outcome, source address, or reset mechanism. The only logging-related behavior is forwarding errors; rejected and successful reset attempts are not logged. This weakens detection and investigation of brute-force reset attacks and account takeover. Logging might be implemented in middleware or model hooks not shown here, so the finding is limited to the visible flow.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: unauthenticated POST /rest/user/reset-password reaches the exported reset handler.
The handler receives the target email and security answer from the request and begins processing a security-sensitive reset attempt.
Failed answer verification returns an HTTP 401 response, but no security event is recorded for the failed attempt.
A valid answer causes the account password to be changed and a user object to be returned, but no audit log or monitoring event is emitted for the successful reset.

title: SQL injection in product search query
description: The unauthenticated product-search handler accepts the `q` query parameter and interpolates it directly into a raw SQL statement. The 200-character truncation limits length but does not parameterize or safely constrain SQL syntax. An attacker can supply SQL metacharacters in `q` to alter the `WHERE` clause, potentially bypassing the intended search predicate and retrieving product records or causing database-side effects, depending on the database configuration.

The handler receives the attacker-controlled `q` query parameter and assigns it to `criteria`; only a length truncation is applied, which is not an SQL injection defense.

The raw SQL query is assembled with a template literal containing `criteria` directly inside `LIKE` expressions and passed to `models.sequelize.query()` without bind parameters or an effective allow-list.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated product search can consume resources
description: The public search endpoint performs an unrestricted raw `SELECT *` search using leading-wildcard `LIKE` predicates and returns every matching product in one response. The input is capped at 200 characters, but there is no result limit, pagination, timeout, or handler-level rate limiting visible here. A broadly matching query such as a short wildcard-compatible term can force repeated full-table scans, large result materialization, translation, serialization, and response generation, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to consume database, CPU, memory, and bandwidth resources.

trace.description: `searchProducts()` is the handler for the unauthenticated `GET /rest/products/search` route; the route registration and any infrastructure controls are outside this file.
The attacker controls the search criteria through `req.query.q`; the code limits only the input length and does not impose a result-count limit or pagination parameters.
Each request executes `SELECT *` with leading-wildcard `LIKE '%...%'` predicates and no `LIMIT`, potentially scanning and materializing all matching products.

title: Unauthenticated and forgeable continuation codes restore arbitrary challenge progress
description: All three restore-progress handlers are reachable without authentication and treat a caller-supplied Hashids value as sufficient authority to mark challenges solved. The salts are hardcoded and the format is reversible/forgeable encoding rather than a cryptographic, user-bound authorization token, so an attacker can generate a valid code for challenge IDs and invoke the endpoint. There is no check binding the decoded IDs or resulting progress to the requesting user, allowing unauthorized progress/state changes and potentially bypassing challenge gates.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives the attacker-controlled `params.continueCode` for the unauthenticated `PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:continueCode` route. No authentication or authorization is performed before processing it.

The handler constructs Hashids with a hardcoded, source-visible salt. Hashids provides encoding/obfuscation, not a cryptographic signature or user binding, so anyone who knows the salt can construct codes for selected challenge IDs.
The route decodes the caller-controlled path value and accepts any syntactically valid decoded ID set without checking an expiry, signature, ownership, or association with the current account.
Every matching challenge is marked solved using the decoded IDs. This is the security-impacting state mutation and occurs without a per-user authorization check.

title: Unauthenticated restore endpoints lack input-size and abuse controls
description: The restore endpoints accept an attacker-controlled path parameter with no application-level length bound or throttling. Hashids must parse the supplied string, after which the handler iterates over every cached challenge and may invoke the challenge-solving logic for each decoded ID. Because the routes are unauthenticated, repeated requests or oversized values can consume CPU and event-loop time and can trigger repeated state-processing work, creating a denial-of-service vector. Deployment-level URI limits or rate limiting may reduce the impact but are not present in this handler.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; an unauthenticated attacker reaches the exported restore handler with an arbitrary `continueCode` path parameter.
The unbounded path value is passed to Hashids decoding after only an alphanumeric-character check; the check does not impose a maximum length or computational budget.

After decoding, the handler scans the complete challenge cache for every request and may perform challenge-solving work for each matching ID, with no rate limit, per-user quota, or request-cost limit.
The attacker-controlled decoded set can cause repeated calls to the challenge-solving operation, providing the expensive state-mutating sink for unauthenticated abuse.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of users' security questions by email
description: The exported handler is registered as unauthenticated GET /rest/user/security-question and accepts an arbitrary email query parameter. It looks up a SecurityAnswer joined to User by that email, without authenticating the requester or checking that the requester owns or is authorized to access the account. If a matching answer exists, the handler returns that user's security question. An attacker can submit another user's email and retrieve the question used in that account's authentication or recovery flow, disclosing an authentication factor and potentially enabling targeted social engineering or downstream security-question attacks.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported handler through unauthenticated GET /rest/user/security-question; the handler receives the Express request and response without any in-file authentication or authorization check.
The handler accepts the caller-controlled query.email value as the account identifier.
The supplied email is used to locate a SecurityAnswer through an associated User record. The lookup is not scoped to an authenticated user and no ownership or role check follows it.
The User association filters by the attacker-selected email, allowing a requester to target another account's security answer record.
After finding a matching record, the handler loads the corresponding security question and returns it to the requester without authorization.

title: Unsanitized client-controlled IP header is persisted and reflected
description: The authenticated endpoint accepts the caller-controlled `true-client-ip` HTTP header and, when `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, deliberately skips `security.sanitizeSecure`. The raw value is persisted as `lastLoginIp` and returned in the JSON response. An attacker can submit a payload such as an HTML/script string in this header; if the stored value is later rendered by a browser-facing client without contextual escaping, this becomes stored XSS. The unsanitized branch is an explicit injection sink, although the final browser-rendering sink is outside this file.

trace.description: GET /rest/saveLoginIp reaches the exported middleware; the route caller is outside this file. The handler receives attacker-controlled request headers through `req`.
The `true-client-ip` header is read directly from the request and normalized only if it is an array; no trust validation is applied to the header value.
When the HTTP-header XSS challenge is enabled, the sanitization branch is empty, so the attacker-controlled header value remains unchanged.

The raw value is written into the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` property and then included in the JSON response. Any downstream browser rendering of this persisted value can execute an injected payload.

title: Client can spoof the stored login IP via true-client-ip
description: The handler treats `true-client-ip` as authoritative input whenever the header is present. A client can provide an arbitrary value, and the fallback to the socket address is used only when the header is absent. This allows authenticated callers to corrupt the recorded login IP, undermining the integrity of audit, security, or fraud-detection decisions that rely on `lastLoginIp`. A reverse proxy that strips or overwrites this header could mitigate the issue, but that control is not visible in this file.

trace.description: GET /rest/saveLoginIp is reachable without route-level auth middleware; the exported handler receives the request from an external caller.
The handler obtains the caller's request-supplied `true-client-ip` header instead of deriving the address from a trusted connection or proxy context.
The socket address is used only when the header is undefined, so any supplied header value takes precedence over the actual peer address.
The caller-controlled value is persisted as `lastLoginIp`, allowing the recorded login-origin metadata to be falsified.

title: Caller-controlled order ID reaches MongoDB $where JavaScript
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/track-order/:id handler uses the caller-controlled path parameter in a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. When reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, the alternate truncation path at line 15 does not restrict quotes or JavaScript syntax, allowing an attacker to break out of the string literal and inject MongoDB JavaScript into the $where predicate at line 17. This can alter query behavior and potentially trigger expensive server-side JavaScript execution or other MongoDB $where impacts.

The path parameter is copied into id. The normal branch applies a restrictive character replacement, but when reflectedXssChallenge is enabled the code only truncates the value and permits quote and JavaScript metacharacters.
