title: Unauthenticated order tracking lacks ownership authorization
description: The route is explicitly registered without authentication, and the handler looks up an order solely by the caller-supplied order ID. There is no check that the requester owns the order or is otherwise authorized to view it before the resulting record is returned. An attacker who obtains or guesses another user's order ID can request that ID and receive the corresponding order data.

trace.description: GET /rest/track-order/:id is an unauthenticated route according to the provided route mapping; the caller and route registration are outside this file.
The target resource identifier is taken directly from req.params.id and normalized into id, with no authenticated user identity or ownership information incorporated.
The database lookup filters only on the supplied orderId and does not constrain the query to the current user, account, or owner.
The first matching order is converted to JSON and returned to the caller without a per-resource authorization check.

title: Attacker-controlled product ID reaches MongoDB $where JavaScript
description: The public GET /rest/products/:id/reviews handler incorporates the path parameter into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression. When the NoSQL command challenge is enabled, `req.params.id` is only truncated to 40 characters; truncation does not constrain the value to a numeric or otherwise safe expression. An attacker can supply JavaScript syntax such as an injected boolean expression or function invocation, causing attacker-controlled code to be evaluated by MongoDB. The normal-mode `Number()` conversion does not protect the challenge-enabled code path.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives the attacker-controlled HTTP request for GET /rest/products/:id/reviews through Express.

The handler reads `req.params.id`. Depending on application state, it either converts the value to a number or merely truncates the raw string to 40 characters; the latter is not an injection-safe allow-list.
The resulting value is concatenated into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression and executed by the database. No parameterization or syntax allow-list intervenes.

title: Unbounded public product-review query enables resource exhaustion
description: This unauthenticated endpoint performs an unbounded MongoDB `find` using a `$where` predicate, then iterates over every matching review and serializes the complete result. There is no pagination, result limit, timeout, or application-level throttling in this handler. Because `$where` requires JavaScript evaluation across candidate documents and the complete result is retained in memory before JSON serialization, repeated requests or a product with a large review set can consume database CPU, application memory, and response bandwidth.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the handler is reachable without authentication at GET /rest/products/:id/reviews.
The request's product identifier is used to construct a database predicate, but the handler does not apply pagination, a result cap, or a query timeout.
The unbounded query result is loaded into `reviews`, processed in a loop, and returned in full as JSON, allowing a single request to consume resources proportional to the matching review count.

title: Authenticated users can modify reviews belonging to other users
description: The authenticated PATCH endpoint accepts a review identifier from `req.body.id` and updates the matching review without checking that the authenticated user owns or authored it. Although the authenticated user is retrieved at line 15, it is never used in the database selector or authorization decision. User A can submit User B's review ID and replace its message, causing unauthorized modification of another user's review. The `{ multi: true }` option further broadens the mutation if the selector matches multiple records.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported handler for PATCH `/rest/products/reviews`; the handler receives attacker-controlled request data through `req.body` and is protected only by the route's authentication middleware.
The handler obtains the authenticated user, but the resulting `user` value is unused and no ownership or author check is constructed from it.
The caller-controlled `req.body.id` is used as the sole review selector. There is no condition tying the selected review to the authenticated user, such as an author or user identifier.
The database update persists the attacker-controlled message to the selected review, with `multi: true` allowing every matching review to be modified.

title: Unvalidated MongoDB selector enables operator injection and bulk review modification
description: The request body field `id` is inserted directly as the value of a MongoDB query selector without enforcing that it is a scalar review ID. If the MongoDB driver accepts operator objects, an attacker can submit a selector such as `{"$in":[...]}` (or another query operator) instead of a single ID. Combined with `multi: true`, this can select and modify multiple reviews in one request, bypassing the intended single-review update semantics and potentially amplifying the access-control issue.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies attacker-controlled JSON in the PATCH request body received by the exported handler.
The body field `id` is passed directly into the MongoDB selector without scalar type validation or an allow-list that rejects MongoDB operator objects.
The selector is executed by `reviewsCollection.update`, interpreting any supplied selector structure as MongoDB query logic rather than enforcing one review identifier.
The `multi: true` option causes all records matching the injected selector to receive the attacker-controlled message, permitting bulk modification and magnifying unauthorized data integrity impact.

title: User-controlled username reaches server-side eval
description: The authenticated user's stored username is treated as executable JavaScript when it matches `#{...}` and the username challenge is enabled. A caller who can create or modify their username can submit a payload such as `#{process.env.SECRET}` or other JavaScript, have it loaded through the profile endpoint, and execute it in the server process via `eval`. This can expose secrets, alter application state, or achieve server-side code execution depending on available runtime capabilities.

trace.description: The exported profile handler receives the HTTP request from the caller outside this file; the route is registered as unauthenticated at the framework level, although the handler performs its own cookie-based session lookup.

The handler retrieves the authenticated user's database record using the session-derived user ID, and then obtains the persisted username. The username is therefore attacker-influenced if the application permits users to choose or change it.
The persisted username is checked for the `#{...}` syntax, the contents are extracted directly, and the resulting string is passed to JavaScript `eval` without an allow-list or safe interpretation.
`eval(code)` executes attacker-influenced username content in the server process, providing a code-injection path.

title: Authentication token cookie lacks security attributes
description: The handler sets the authentication token in a response cookie without any security attributes. Express does not add HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite by default when res.cookie is called without options. Consequently, client-side script can read the session token, and the token may be transmitted over plaintext HTTP if the deployment permits it. The absence of an explicit SameSite policy also removes a defense-in-depth control for this state-changing endpoint.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported profile-update handler through POST /profile; the route is declared without authentication middleware, so this function itself is responsible for the session check.
The handler authenticates the request using the token supplied in req.cookies.token and loads the associated user.

After updating the profile, the handler places the newly issued authentication token in a cookie without HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, or any other security options. Express defaults do not supply these attributes.

title: Cookie-authenticated profile mutation lacks visible CSRF protection
description: POST /profile performs an authenticated state-changing profile update, but this handler has no CSRF token validation, origin validation, or other request-origin check. Authentication relies on a browser cookie, so a cross-site request may cause the victim's username to be changed if the browser sends the session cookie. The route is declared with no authentication or authorization middleware, and the only visible checks are the cookie lookup and existence check.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported handler for POST /profile; the route has no declared authentication or authorization middleware.
The handler accepts the browser cookie as its authentication mechanism and only verifies that the token maps to a logged-in user; it does not validate the request origin or a CSRF token.

The caller-controlled username is persisted through a state-changing update. A cross-site request carrying the victim's cookie can therefore modify the victim's profile when browser cookie policy permits the request.

title: Profile update endpoint has no visible rate limiting
description: The profile-update endpoint performs a database write and token/session update for every request, but this file shows no per-IP, per-user, or per-endpoint rate limiting. An attacker with a valid session, or a victim whose browser can be induced to make repeated requests, can generate unbounded profile writes and token-cookie updates, consuming database and application resources. Infrastructure-level throttling cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported handler through POST /profile; no rate-limiting middleware is listed for the route.
Each request reads attacker-influenced request state and proceeds through the authenticated profile mutation path without any local request-count or frequency check.
Every accepted request performs a persistent UserModel update, converts the result, creates a new authorization token, and stores it in the in-memory authenticated-user map.

title: Profile changes are not auditable in the handler
description: Changing a username is an account/profile security-relevant event, but this handler contains no audit log for successful changes or for rejected unauthenticated attempts. Without logging at this path, operators cannot reliably detect or investigate unauthorized or abusive profile modifications. Logging may exist in unseen middleware or model hooks, which is why confidence is limited.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported POST /profile handler, which processes an account profile mutation.
Unauthenticated attempts are passed to next with an error, but no security event is recorded; successful requests likewise continue without audit instrumentation.
The username is persisted and the session is refreshed without any log or audit event identifying the profile change or its outcome.

title: Unauthenticated promotion endpoint performs expensive work on every request
description: The unauthenticated promotion endpoint performs synchronous filesystem I/O and recompiles a Pug template on every request. A remote client can repeatedly request GET /promotion, causing blocking disk reads of the template and subtitle file, dynamic template compilation, and per-request memory/CPU consumption. No rate limiting, caching, or other request-level control is visible in this handler.

trace.description: GET /promotion reaches this exported handler; the route caller and any upstream throttling are outside this file.
Each request asynchronously reads the promotion template from disk before generating the response.
The request also synchronously reads the configured subtitle file, blocking the event loop and loading the entire file into memory.
The handler dynamically imports Pug and compiles the template for each request rather than reusing a precompiled template, creating an avoidable CPU and memory sink reachable without authentication.

title: Promotion subtitle path permits configuration-driven directory traversal
description: The configured subtitle filename is concatenated directly into the promotion asset path without the filename sanitization applied to the video configuration. If an attacker can influence application.promotion.subtitles through deployment configuration, an environment/configuration-management weakness, or another configuration write path, values containing ../ can escape the intended video directory. Because the resulting file contents are returned as part of the public /promotion response, this can disclose arbitrary readable local files. The external ability to modify this configuration is not shown in this file.

trace.description: GET /promotion invokes this handler without authentication; the route registration is outside this file.
The handler obtains subtitle content while constructing the public promotion response.
The subtitle filename is read from application.promotion.subtitles and is not passed through utils.extractFilename or another visible allow-list.

The unvalidated value is concatenated into a filesystem path and synchronously read. ../ segments can escape frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/videos, after which the contents are embedded into the response.

title: Unbounded selectedLines enables resource-exhaustion requests
description: The unauthenticated POST /snippets/verdict handler accepts selectedLines directly from the request body and performs repeated linear membership checks over it. getVerdict calls selectedLines.includes once for every vulnerable line and then iterates over the entire selectedLines array, with no length cap, complexity bound, or per-request throttling in this file. An attacker can submit an extremely large array, or repeatedly invoke the public endpoint, causing excessive CPU and request-body memory consumption and potentially degrading service availability.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives unauthenticated POST /snippets/verdict requests and reads the attacker-controlled request body.
The handler copies req.body.selectedLines into selectedLines without validating that it has a reasonable maximum length.
The attacker-controlled array is passed into getVerdict for processing.

getVerdict performs selectedLines.includes for each vulnerable line and then scans the complete selectedLines array with filter/includes. The work and memory consumed are proportional to attacker-controlled input, with no local size limit or throttling control.

title: Unauthenticated challenge completion state change
description: The unauthenticated POST /snippets/fixes route invokes a state-changing challenge-completion operation. The caller can provide an arbitrary challenge key and, after selecting the expected fix index, cause solveFixIt(key) to mark that challenge as solved without any authentication or authorization check in this handler or route. This permits anonymous or lower-privileged callers to alter challenge/progress state and potentially complete challenges on behalf of another user, depending on how solveFixIt persists progress.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller is outside this file; POST /snippets/fixes is registered with no authentication middleware and reaches checkCorrectFix().
The handler accepts the caller-controlled key and selectedFix values and loads the corresponding fix data without establishing an authenticated identity or checking authorization for the challenge.
When the caller supplies the correct index, the handler performs the state-changing solveFixIt operation. No per-user authorization or other access-control check is present before this operation.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled code-fix cache
description: The unauthenticated GET /snippets/fixes/:key endpoint accepts an attacker-controlled key and passes every distinct value to a process-global cache. Missing keys are also cached, so an attacker can issue requests with continuously changing keys to grow CodeFixes without bound. Each uncached request additionally performs synchronous directory enumeration and may read matching files, consuming memory and filesystem/CPU resources until the process degrades or exhausts memory.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller is outside this file; unauthenticated GET /snippets/fixes/:key supplies an arbitrary path parameter to serveCodeFixes().
The route value is passed directly to readFixes(), which checks the process-global CodeFixes cache and, for a new key, performs synchronous directory enumeration and file processing.

For every previously unseen key, including keys for which no fixes exist, the handler stores a new entry in the global cache. There is no size bound, eviction policy, rate limit, or validation/allow-list limiting the key space.

title: Unbounded global CAPTCHA request tracking enables memory exhaustion
description: The CAPTCHA-related middleware mutates process-wide state for every unauthenticated POST /api/Feedbacks request but applies no rate limit, quota, expiration, or maximum index. An attacker can repeatedly invoke the public route, causing captchaBypassReqTimes to grow and captchaReqId to increase indefinitely, consuming memory and eventually degrading or exhausting the process.

trace.description: External callers reach this exported middleware through the unauthenticated POST /api/Feedbacks route; the caller and route handler are outside this file.
Each request writes a timestamp into the global captchaBypassReqTimes array at an ever-advancing index, with no bound or cleanup visible in this middleware.
The global request ID is incremented for every request without a cap, allowing repeated unauthenticated requests to create unbounded state and then pass to the handler.

title: Access-control challenge is calculated but never enforced
description: accessControlChallenges computes whether a request should be considered UI-bypassed, but the result is never used. Every request, including requests that do not meet the apparent UI condition, is passed to the next handler without any access-control decision. The route using the middleware is outside the supplied file, so the impact depends on whether downstream handlers rely on this middleware as their enforcement point.

trace.description: The exported middleware receives an external Express request; its caller and any protected route are outside this file.
The middleware derives a uiBypassed value from attacker-influenced request headers, but does not use that value to authorize or reject the request.
The unconditional next() passes the request onward regardless of the computed access-control condition.

title: Unauthenticated admin-registration challenge is a no-op
description: POST /api/Users is declared without authentication and invokes registerAdminChallenge, but this middleware performs no role check, request validation, or rejection before forwarding the request. If the external registration handler permits an admin role or otherwise relies on this challenge for privileged-registration protection, an unauthenticated caller can reach that behavior. The downstream handler is not present, so the privilege impact cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

trace.description: The external caller reaches this middleware through the unauthenticated POST /api/Users route; the registration handler is outside this file.
The middleware unconditionally calls next() and therefore provides no server-side enforcement for the admin-registration challenge before the public registration handler executes.

title: Password-repeat validation middleware is bypassable
description: The password-repeat challenge attached to unauthenticated POST /api/Users does not inspect the request body or compare the repeated password with the original password. It unconditionally forwards the request. If the external registration handler expects this middleware to enforce password confirmation, callers can omit or mismatch the confirmation field and still reach registration.

trace.description: An external registration request reaches this exported middleware through the unauthenticated POST /api/Users route; the caller and registration handler are outside this file.
The middleware performs no comparison or validation and unconditionally forwards the request, leaving the password-repeat workflow unenforced at this point.

title: Unbounded prompt-similarity inputs permit CPU and memory exhaustion
description: The exported similarity checker accepts caller-provided strings without any length limit. It allocates a Map entry for every bigram in the submission and then iterates over the reference, so a reachable endpoint that forwards attacker-controlled large strings can force linear memory and CPU consumption per request. No truncation, maximum input size, or throttling is present in this file.

trace.description: The exported diceCoefficient function receives strings from an external caller; the caller and any route exposing it are outside this file.
The function constructs a bigram map from the entire submission, with work and retained entries proportional to the input length.
Each input bigram is inserted into the Map without a size cap, allowing very large attacker-controlled submissions to consume memory and processing time.

title: Caller-controlled wallet balance increment enables arbitrary credit manipulation
description: The wallet top-up amount is taken directly from the caller-controlled `req.body.balance` and passed to `WalletModel.increment` without validating that it is a positive, bounded monetary value or confirming the amount against an actual payment transaction. A user with any accepted stored card can submit an arbitrarily large amount to create wallet credit, or submit a negative amount to decrement the wallet balance. This permits direct manipulation of the wallet's financial state.

trace.description: PUT /rest/wallet/balance invokes the exported handler; the route is protected by `security.appendUserId()` outside this file, while request fields including `balance` enter through the handler's `req.body`.

The handler reads `req.body.paymentId` and uses it only to verify that the referenced card belongs to `req.body.UserId`; this establishes possession of a stored card but does not establish that the caller is authorized to choose an arbitrary top-up amount.

The caller-controlled `req.body.balance` is passed directly as the increment value. There is no positive-value check, upper bound, currency/precision validation, or server-side derivation from a payment authorization.

title: Wallet ownership is selected from request-body UserId
description: Both handlers derive the wallet owner from `req.body.UserId`, a request-body property, rather than from an immutable authenticated-user context. The route's `appendUserId()` middleware may overwrite this field, but that behavior is outside the file and cannot be confirmed here. If it merely appends the field or permits a supplied value to survive, an authenticated user can substitute another user's ID to read that user's balance or mutate that user's wallet, creating a BOLA/access-control flaw.

trace.description: GET /rest/wallet/balance and PUT /rest/wallet/balance reach these exported handlers through `security.appendUserId()` middleware declared outside this file; the caller and middleware implementation are external to this trace.
The wallet lookup uses `req.body.UserId` as the owner identifier. No handler-local check compares this value with a trusted authenticated principal.
The mutation similarly scopes the card lookup and wallet update using `req.body.UserId`; if that body field is attacker-controlled, the attacker can target another user's wallet.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint enables unbounded wallet-state and WebSocket resource consumption
description: The unauthenticated POST handler accepts an arbitrary `walletAddress` and inserts it into the process-wide `walletsConnected` Set without validation, expiration, eviction, or a size limit. An attacker can submit many requests containing distinct wallet addresses, causing the Set to grow for the lifetime of the process and consume memory. Additionally, concurrent requests can all observe `isEventListenerCreated` as false before awaiting the dynamic import/provider setup, causing multiple WebSocket providers and contract event listeners to be created, further increasing resource consumption. This can degrade or exhaust application memory and outbound WebSocket resources.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is registered as unauthenticated `POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress`, so any remote caller can invoke it.
The handler reads attacker-controlled `req.body.walletAddress` and adds it to a process-wide Set. There is no type, format, cardinality, expiration, or eviction check.

For each request that observes the listener flag as false, the handler dynamically imports ethers and creates a new WebSocket provider. The asynchronous setup permits concurrent requests to enter this branch before the flag is set.

The handler creates a contract event subscription backed by the newly created provider. Repeated or racing requests can therefore allocate persistent WebSocket connections/listeners, while the unbounded Set retains attacker-supplied addresses.

title: Hardcoded and reused TOTP secrets in authentication tests
description: The test source contains reusable hardcoded TOTP secrets, including the secret for the `wurstbrot` account and a shared setup secret reused across multiple newly registered accounts. These values are used to generate valid one-time passwords and are also passed into 2FA setup flows. If these fixtures or their credentials are reachable in a deployed or shared test environment, anyone who obtains the source can generate valid MFA codes and complete or disable 2FA for the corresponding accounts. Even if limited to tests, embedding authentication secrets in source encourages reuse and can expose live or persistent test accounts.

trace.description: The `/rest/2fa/verify` test workflow executes requests against the application; the attacker-facing application route is defined outside this file, while this file supplies authentication material to that route.
A fixed TOTP secret is embedded in the test source and used to generate a currently valid TOTP value for the `wurstbrot` account.
The generated TOTP and temporary authentication token are submitted to `/rest/2fa/verify`, and the test expects an authenticated response for the account.
The 2FA setup workflow also embeds the fixed secret `KDR5FXSOLNV6A5UAQYCKROSJZF7SVML7` and uses it to generate the initial enrollment token.

The hardcoded secret is supplied to the setup endpoint as the authoritative setup secret and can be reused to generate valid enrollment codes; the same value is repeated for multiple test accounts elsewhere in this file.

title: Test accepts unauthenticated access to administrative configuration endpoint
description: The administration test invokes `GET /rest/admin/application-configuration` without supplying any authentication or authorization credentials and explicitly requires a successful 200 response. This codifies and potentially regression-tests unauthenticated access to an administrative configuration endpoint. If the test app mirrors production routing, an unauthenticated attacker could retrieve internal application configuration, potentially exposing deployment details or security-sensitive settings. The route implementation and middleware are outside this file, so the exact exposure cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The test creates the application instance via `createTestApp`; the underlying route and authentication configuration are outside this file.
The test sends a request to the administrative configuration endpoint without an Authorization header, session cookie, or other credentials.
The test asserts HTTP 200 and therefore treats successful unauthenticated retrieval of the administrative configuration as expected behavior.

title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials used for authentication
description: The test suite embeds a reusable username and plaintext password directly in source code and uses them to obtain an authenticated bearer token. If this fixture account exists in a shared, deployed, or otherwise reachable environment, anyone with access to the repository can authenticate as that user and access or modify address resources. Test-only credentials should be isolated to disposable environments and supplied through test configuration or generated fixtures rather than committed plaintext credentials.

trace.description: The test receives the application instance from createTestApp; the application setup and account provisioning are outside this file.
The test passes a fixed email address to the login helper to obtain an authentication token.
The test passes the plaintext password `ncc-1701` to the login helper. This committed credential is the sink because it can be reused by anyone who can reach the corresponding account.

title: Privileged-account password hint exposed in public JavaScript bundle
description: The test confirms that the publicly requested `/main.js` bundle contains a password-policy hint for privileged support-team accounts. Exposing account-related password hints in client-delivered JavaScript gives unauthenticated users information that may assist password guessing or account targeting, and indicates that internal account security details are being treated as public frontend content. The test does not establish whether the hint is the actual password, so the impact is primarily information disclosure.

trace.description: The test acts as an external caller by issuing an unauthenticated request for the client bundle; the served application is outside this test file.
The request targets the publicly served `/main.js` resource.

The assertion requires the response body to contain a message stating that the support team's password violates the policy for privileged accounts and should be changed, confirming that this internal security-related hint is embedded in the public bundle.

title: Continue-code workflow accepts codes for non-existent challenges
description: The public continue-code workflow accepts a continue code associated with a non-existent challenge and returns HTTP 200. This permits callers to submit a syntactically valid code for challenge state that the server cannot resolve, indicating that the workflow does not enforce the invariant that every applied code must correspond to an existing challenge. Depending on the downstream state update, an attacker may create invalid solved-challenge state or bypass expected challenge progression. The test explicitly locks in this behavior rather than rejecting it.

trace.description: HTTP PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:code is exercised through the test request; the route handler is outside this file, and the path parameter is the caller-supplied continue code.
The request submits a continue code intended to represent challenge state, including the test case's non-existent challenge #999 scenario.
The test asserts that the server returns 200 for the non-existent-challenge code, demonstrating acceptance rather than rejecting unresolved challenge state.

title: Basket item can be assigned to an arbitrary basket through an omitted initial BasketId
description: The basket-item workflow permits a caller to create an item without assigning it to a basket, then later assign it to an arbitrary basket identifier. The adjacent tests show that BasketId is rejected as an update when the item already has one, but the same property is accepted when initially omitted. If the supplied BasketId belongs to another user, this enables cross-basket placement or manipulation and bypasses the intended immutable-basket invariant.

trace.description: The attacker-facing workflow is the authenticated POST /api/BasketItems followed by PUT /api/BasketItems/:id; the route implementation is outside this test file.
The POST request creates a basket item without supplying BasketId, and the test confirms the server accepts the item with an undefined basket association.
The caller then submits PUT /api/BasketItems/:id with BasketId set to 3, despite the model's noUpdate behavior being intended to prevent basket reassignment.

The server returns success and the response contains BasketId 3, demonstrating that the caller-controlled basket association was applied without any ownership or valid-transition assertion visible in this file.

title: Plaintext test account credential committed in source
description: The test suite contains a plaintext password for the jim@juice-sh.op account. Anyone with access to the repository can obtain this credential and authenticate wherever the seeded or shared test account is reachable. Although it may be intended only for test environments, committing reusable credentials is an insecure configuration and can become an access path if test deployments are exposed or credentials are reused.

The login identity is hardcoded as jim@juice-sh.op, establishing a reusable account credential in source-controlled test code.
The plaintext password ncc-1701 is passed directly to login and can be recovered by anyone who can read the repository.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key in test source
description: The test source contains a hardcoded Ethereum private key and sends it as the `privateKey` request field. Anyone with access to the repository or built test artifacts can recover and reuse this credential, potentially controlling the associated wallet if it holds assets or has signing authority. Although this appears to be a test fixture, private keys should be generated for isolated tests or replaced with a demonstrably unusable fixture.

trace.description: The test runner executes a test that exercises the wallet-unlock endpoint using a private key; the caller is outside this file.
The test embeds a complete 32-byte Ethereum private key directly in the request body.

title: Hardcoded account credentials in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext credentials for seeded accounts, including an account likely associated with an administrator (`bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com`) and another user account. These values are passed directly to the authentication helper and become reusable credentials for any environment where the corresponding accounts exist. Although this is a test file, committing reusable authentication material to source creates credential exposure and can enable unauthorized login if test or shared environments are reachable.

The login call supplies a hardcoded email address and plaintext password, rather than obtaining credentials from protected test configuration or ephemeral account provisioning.
A second authenticated test also embeds a plaintext password for another seeded account, confirming that reusable authentication credentials are stored directly in the repository.

title: Exposed mock LLM server accepts unbounded request bodies
description: The test suite starts an unauthenticated HTTP mock server on a fixed port without binding it to a loopback-only interface. It reads request bodies by repeatedly concatenating every received chunk into an in-memory string and applies no body-size limit. A client able to reach port 43210 can send an arbitrarily large request body, causing unbounded memory growth and potentially exhausting the test or CI process. Binding the mock server broadly also exposes an internal test service beyond the local process.

trace.description: The test suite creates a network listener on a fixed port without specifying a loopback host, so the mock service may be reachable from other hosts depending on the runtime network configuration.
The server accepts incoming requests and routes POST requests resembling chat-completion calls to the configurable LLM request handler without authentication.
Every request data chunk is converted to a string and appended to one accumulator with no maximum body size, content-length check, timeout, or other memory bound.
The accumulated attacker-controlled body is passed to the request handler; subsequent handlers parse it, allowing a sufficiently large body to consume memory before processing completes.

title: Authenticated users can read other users' baskets by ID
description: An authenticated user can retrieve another user's basket by supplying its numeric identifier. The test logs in as the account associated with basket 2, requests `/rest/basket/2`, and receives the basket with ID 2 and HTTP 200. No ownership check is evidenced between authentication and returning the requested basket, enabling BOLA/data disclosure.

trace.description: The attacker-facing GET `/rest/basket/:id` request is issued by an authenticated caller; the route handler is outside this file.
The caller supplies basket identifier `2` in the URL while authenticating with the token obtained for another account.
The response is 200 and contains basket ID 2, demonstrating that authentication is accepted without per-basket ownership authorization.

title: Basket coupon and checkout operations lack ownership enforcement
description: The authenticated user represented by `authHeader` can apply a coupon to basket 2 and place an order for that basket. The test explicitly performs the coupon mutation and checkout using an authenticated token, with both operations succeeding. Because basket 2 is established as another user's basket in the preceding test, the identifier is not scoped to the current user, permitting unauthorized modification and purchase of another user's basket.

trace.description: The attacker-facing PUT `/rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon` and POST `/rest/basket/:id/checkout` operations are invoked by an authenticated caller; their handlers are outside this file.
The caller targets basket `2` with its authenticated token and the coupon endpoint returns 200 with a 99% discount.
The response confirms the discount was applied to basket 2, showing an unauthorized state mutation is accepted.
The same authenticated caller then checks out basket 2 and receives a successful order confirmation.

title: Forged coupon accepted for a 99% discount
description: A coupon identified by the test as forged is accepted with a 99% discount and can then be used for checkout. The coupon-generation and validation implementation is outside this file, so the precise cryptographic weakness cannot be established here; however, the observed behavior demonstrates a coupon-integrity/business-rule bypass that allows near-free orders.

trace.description: The test constructs a value explicitly named `forgedCoupon` using the coupon-generation helper; the helper implementation is outside this file.
The forged value is supplied as the coupon path parameter for basket 2.
The application accepts the value and reports a 99% discount.
The discounted basket is successfully checked out, producing an order confirmation.

title: HTTP 500 responses disclose internal exception messages
description: Error responses expose raw internal exception messages. The tests inject failures from quantity, wallet, and order-insert operations and assert that strings such as `Quantity error`, `Wallet error`, and `Insert error` appear in the HTTP response body. If the same error handling is enabled outside the test environment, attackers can use these responses to enumerate backend components and implementation details.

The test forces an internal `QuantityModel.findOne` failure, demonstrating that backend exceptions reach the request path.
The response body is asserted to contain the raw internal error text, confirming exception-message exposure in the HTTP response.

title: Hardcoded administrative credentials in source

The contract performs the token payout without emitting any event identifying the caller, requested amount, or transfer result. No logging event is declared anywhere in the file.

title: Unbounded owner-controlled minting permits arbitrary inflation
description: The token exposes an owner-authorized minting function with no maximum supply, rate limit, governance requirement, or other compensating control. The deployer is permanently recorded as `_owner`, and that account can repeatedly call `mintTokens` to create an arbitrary number of tokens for any recipient. If the token is intended to represent a fixed or bounded supply, a compromised or malicious owner can arbitrarily inflate supply, dilute holders, and manipulate the token economy.

trace.description: External callers can invoke `mintTokens(address recipient, uint256 amount)`; the caller is outside this file. The function accepts an arbitrary recipient and amount and is reachable by the recorded owner.
After the `onlyOwner` check, the caller-supplied recipient and amount are forwarded directly to `_mint` without any supply cap or other business-rule validation.
`_mint` increases `_totalSupply` and the recipient balance by the arbitrary amount. Repeated authorized calls can therefore create unlimited tokens and dilute existing holders.

title: NFT minted without verifying ERC-20 payment success
description: The mint workflow treats the ERC-20 payment as successful without checking the boolean result of `transferFrom`. An ERC-20 token is permitted to return `false` instead of reverting when the transfer cannot be completed. Because the return value is ignored, execution proceeds to `_safeMint`, allowing an attacker to receive an NFT without paying the required `mintPrice` when the configured token returns `false` (or uses a non-reverting failure path).

trace.description: Entrypoint: `mintNFT()` is externally callable; the caller is outside this file and supplies the transaction sender used as the payment source and NFT recipient.

The function requests `mintPrice` tokens from `msg.sender` via the configured external ERC-20 contract, but ignores the `bool` return value from `transferFrom`. A false return therefore does not stop the workflow.
The contract mints the NFT to `msg.sender` regardless of whether the preceding token transfer succeeded, creating the business-logic imbalance that enables free minting.

title: Reentrant withdrawals can drain ETH and cause balance underflow
description: The withdrawal workflow performs an external call before decrementing the caller's balance. An attacker-controlled contract can call withdraw for an amount equal to the victim contract's entire recorded balance, reenter from its fallback during line 31, and pass the balance check again because the balance has not yet been reduced. Both calls then transfer funds. When the nested call executes line 33, Solidity 0.6.x performs unchecked arithmetic for the raw subtraction, so subtracting the same amount from a zero balance wraps the balance to a very large uint256 value. The attacker can therefore withdraw more ETH than was credited to its account and inflate its recorded balance.

trace.description: The public withdraw function receives attacker-controlled amount and caller context; the external attacker-facing caller or attacker contract is outside this file.
The function checks the current balance before making any external call, but does not reserve or deduct the amount before transferring funds.
The contract sends ETH to msg.sender via a low-level external call while the balance update is still pending. A malicious recipient contract can reenter withdraw from its fallback.

The balance is decremented only after the external call and uses unchecked raw subtraction in Solidity 0.6.12. Repeated withdrawals can therefore underflow the balance and create an artificially large credit.

title: Normal deposits and withdrawals lack security-relevant audit events
description: Normal deposits and successful withdrawals do not emit audit events. The only event is ContractExploited, which is emitted only on the reentrancy-detection path and does not provide a reliable audit trail for ordinary fund movements. Off-chain monitoring systems that consume contract events cannot reliably reconstruct deposits, withdrawals, amounts, or affected accounts from the contract's security-relevant logs, reducing the ability to detect and investigate unauthorized fund movement.

trace.description: The public deposit function receives a value transfer and recipient address from a caller outside this file.
The deposit changes a user's recorded balance but emits no deposit event containing the sender, recipient, or amount.
The public withdrawal function is another security-relevant fund-transfer entrypoint, but its ordinary execution path also has no audit event.
After transferring ETH and changing the balance, the successful withdrawal path resets state without emitting a withdrawal event; ContractExploited is not emitted for ordinary withdrawals.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key exposes encrypted data
description: The RSA private modulus/exponent are hardcoded in the source at lines 5-6. The script uses these values to decrypt every integer read from the local announcement file and prints the resulting plaintext. Anyone with access to this source can use the exposed private parameters to decrypt ciphertext intended for the corresponding RSA key, compromising confidentiality and making the cryptographic protection ineffective. The hardcoded private key is also a security misconfiguration because secret key material is embedded in source code.

trace.description: The script receives ciphertext from the fixed local file `announcement_encrypted.md`; the caller or process that places this file is outside the analyzed file.
The decryption operation uses the hardcoded RSA private parameters `d` and `N` declared in source, exposing the private key to anyone who can read the repository.
Each input line is converted to an integer and decrypted with `pow(int(...), d, N)`, then the resulting plaintext is emitted to standard output.

title: Textbook RSA encryption without padding or authentication
description: The file implements textbook RSA directly, encrypting each plaintext character independently with a public exponent and modulus. There is no randomized padding such as RSA-OAEP and no integrity/authentication mechanism. Because the plaintext domain is small and encryption is deterministic, an observer can build a character-to-ciphertext dictionary, identify repeated characters and patterns, and recover substantial plaintext structure. The scheme is therefore unsuitable for confidential document encryption and is vulnerable to ciphertext analysis and tampering.

trace.description: Module execution opens the plaintext document for encryption; the caller/entrypoint is implicit and outside this file.
The implementation uses a fixed public RSA modulus and exponent directly, without selecting a randomized padding scheme or authenticated encryption construction.
The plaintext is read character-by-character, ensuring each character is processed independently rather than encrypting a complete message with randomized, semantically secure encoding.

Each character is transformed with raw modular exponentiation and written as a ciphertext integer. Identical plaintext characters always produce identical ciphertexts, enabling frequency and dictionary analysis; the ciphertext also has no integrity protection.

title: Deterministic textbook RSA enables codebook decryption
description: The script implements textbook, deterministic RSA over individual characters rather than using randomized padding or a private-key decryption operation. It precomputes the ciphertext for every character in a small known alphabet using the public exponent and modulus (lines 10-12), then directly maps each ciphertext value from the input file back to its plaintext character (line 15). Anyone who obtains the encrypted announcement can reproduce the same codebook without any secret key and recover its contents, including by matching repeated ciphertext values. This is exploitable whenever the encrypted file is intended to provide confidentiality.

trace.description: The script's caller is outside this file; execution opens the externally supplied or replaceable local file `announcement_encrypted.md` and uses its contents as ciphertext input.
Before processing the ciphertext, the script defines a small, fixed plaintext alphabet consisting of printable characters plus whitespace, making exhaustive codebook construction feasible.

For every character, the script computes raw RSA encryption with the public exponent and modulus and stores the resulting ciphertext-to-character mapping. No randomized padding, secret key, or authentication mechanism is used.

The input ciphertext is looked up directly in the precomputed public codebook and the recovered plaintext is printed, allowing anyone able to read the encrypted file to decrypt it without possessing a private key.

title: Unpinned Alpine base image and package dependency
description: The image uses mutable, unpinned external dependencies: the base image is referenced only as `alpine`, and `curl` is installed without a version constraint. A rebuild can therefore silently receive different base-image or package contents, including newly introduced vulnerabilities or a compromised/retagged upstream artifact. This weakens build integrity and prevents reliable security patch verification.

trace.description: The Docker build begins by resolving the mutable `alpine` tag from an external image registry; the caller/build pipeline is outside this file.
The image installs `curl` from the default Alpine repositories without pinning a package version or repository snapshot, introducing another mutable external dependency.
The resulting image is built from dependency versions that can change between builds, so a later build may incorporate an unexpected or vulnerable base image/package.

title: Unvalidated smoke-test URL enables arbitrary internal requests
description: The script treats its first positional argument as a trusted service URL and issues several unrestricted curl requests to it and to derived paths. A caller outside this file that can influence $1 can point the smoke test at arbitrary hosts or URL schemes, causing the CI/test runner's network position to access internal services or trigger GET-based actions. The value is shell-quoted, so this is not command injection, but there is no allowlist, scheme restriction, host validation, or protection against internal destinations.

trace.description: The script receives the target URL through positional parameter $1; the caller and any validation of this value are outside this file.
The externally supplied URL is reused to construct multiple request targets, including API and static-resource paths, without restricting the destination or protocol.
curl makes the request using the caller-controlled target. No host allowlist, private-network block, scheme restriction, or other SSRF-style control is present.

title: Curl requests have no timeout and can hang the smoke test indefinitely
description: All four curl invocations lack connection, transfer, or overall execution timeouts. Because the destination is supplied externally, a reachable caller can provide a slow or nonresponsive endpoint and cause the smoke-test process, and potentially the CI job running it, to wait indefinitely. This is a deployment/test-runner availability risk caused by an unsafe network-client configuration.

trace.description: The script accepts a target URL from $1; the invoking job or caller is outside this file and controls which endpoint is contacted.
The supplied URL is used for repeated HTTP checks, so an unresponsive or deliberately slow target can keep the script active across the entire test sequence.
curl is invoked without --connect-timeout, --max-time, or an equivalent timeout option, leaving the request duration unbounded.

title: Unpinned Docker image permits supply-chain substitution
description: The provisioning script starts the Juice Shop container with a mutable image reference (`bkimminich/juice-shop`) and no digest or version pin. Docker will resolve this tag at provisioning time, so a registry-side tag change or compromised image publication can cause a newly provisioned host to execute attacker-controlled code with the container's default privileges. This creates a supply-chain and reproducibility misconfiguration.

trace.description: The script installs and configures Docker, establishing the runtime used for the application.
The deployment flow reaches Docker image retrieval and container creation; the image is selected from an external registry.
The container is started from the mutable `bkimminich/juice-shop` tag without a version or content digest, allowing the image contents to change between provisioning runs.

title: Container service exposed on all host interfaces
description: The container port is published as `3000:3000`, which binds the service on all host interfaces by default. This exposes the application directly to any reachable network client and provides a path that bypasses Apache's front-end configuration and any controls that may be applied there. The file does not restrict the bind address or limit access with a firewall rule.

trace.description: The script installs and starts Apache as the host-facing web server, suggesting that Apache is intended to front the application.
Apache proxy support is enabled and the service is restarted, establishing a separate front-end path whose controls can be bypassed by direct access to the published container port.
Docker publishes container port 3000 to host port 3000 without an address restriction such as `127.0.0.1:3000:3000`; Docker therefore exposes it on all host interfaces.

title: Mutable base images and ranged build dependencies are not pinned
description: The image build relies on mutable, non-digest-pinned external inputs. Both the installer image (`node:24`) and runtime image (`gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13`) are resolved by tags, so a tag update or registry compromise can silently change the toolchain or runtime contents on a later build. The build also installs packages from version ranges (`typescript@^6.0.3` and the CycloneDX range), further weakening reproducibility and supply-chain integrity. An attacker who can influence the referenced registry/tag or dependency resolution can cause a build to incorporate altered code.

trace.description: The Docker build accepts the externally hosted `node:24` installer image by mutable tag; the image reference and its registry resolution are outside this file's control.
The build installs a globally ranged TypeScript package, allowing the resolved toolchain to change between builds.
The SBOM generator is also selected using a version range rather than an immutable version.
The final runtime image is likewise selected by the mutable `nodejs24-debian13` tag rather than a digest, allowing a changed or compromised tag to enter production images.

title: Dependency lifecycle scripts execute as root during the build
description: Dependency installation occurs in the default root context of the installer stage. `npm install` and global package installation can execute dependency lifecycle scripts, so a compromised or malicious package can run arbitrary commands with root privileges during the image build and modify files that are later copied into the runtime image. The runtime process is non-root, but that does not prevent build-time code execution from tampering with the application artifact.

trace.description: The installer stage starts from a Node image without defining a non-root build user, so subsequent commands run as root by default.
The complete application source and package metadata are copied into the root-owned installer environment before dependency installation.

`npm install --omit=dev` may execute package lifecycle scripts with the installer-stage root privileges, allowing a compromised dependency to alter the build workspace or run arbitrary build-time commands.
The global CycloneDX installation is another npm installation performed in the same privileged installer stage and can likewise execute lifecycle scripts as root.

title: Release archive contains private key material
description: The packaging task explicitly includes likely sensitive key material in the distributable archive: `ctf.key` and every file under `encryptionkeys/**`. Any recipient of the generated package can extract these files and potentially use them to forge challenge tokens, decrypt protected data, or impersonate services depending on how the keys are used. Including private key material in a release artifact is an unsafe packaging configuration unless these files are demonstrably non-secret test fixtures.

trace.description: The exported Grunt configuration function receives the `grunt` object from a caller outside this file; invoking the package task causes the configuration below to be evaluated.
The `package` task invokes `compress:pckg`, which builds the release archive from the configured file list.
The archive configuration includes the top-level `ctf.key` file and the complete `encryptionkeys/**` directory.
The same release archive also includes all files matching `encryptionkeys/**`, so newly added key files are implicitly packaged without an explicit allow-list.

title: Release package exposes broad internal source and configuration files
description: The release archive includes broad internal application content, including `config/*.yml`, `data/*.ts`, `frontend/src/**/*.ts`, `models/*.ts`, `routes/*.ts`, `views/**`, `ftp/**`, and the entire `node_modules/**` tree. This can disclose deployment configuration, source code, implementation details, test or operational data, and dependency metadata to every package recipient. The implicit glob-based inclusion also means newly added files in these directories can become public release contents without a security review.

trace.description: The exported Grunt configuration function is called by a caller outside this file and defines the package build.
The `package` task invokes the configured compression target to create the distributable archive.
The compression input uses broad recursive globs for configuration, source, views, FTP content, and the complete `node_modules` directory, with only `build/reports/**` explicitly excluded.
Additional broad globs include application TypeScript sources, models, routes, frontend sources, and all dependencies in `node_modules/**`.

title: Release artifacts use collision-broken MD5 checksums
description: The checksum task generates MD5 checksums for every file in `dist/`. MD5 is collision-broken and is not suitable for security-sensitive artifact integrity verification. An attacker able to provide or substitute a package can exploit MD5 collision weaknesses, and a consumer that treats the adjacent `.md5` file as an authenticity or tamper-proofing mechanism receives no strong integrity assurance. A modern cryptographic hash such as SHA-256, preferably combined with a trusted signature, should be used.

trace.description: The exported Grunt function registers a checksum task that can be invoked by the caller outside this file.
The task enumerates every file in the `dist/` directory and reads each artifact into memory.
Each artifact is hashed with `crypto.createHash('md5')`, selecting the broken MD5 algorithm for integrity metadata.
The resulting MD5 digest is written as a neighboring `.md5` file, creating the integrity record consumers may rely on.

title: Unauthenticated LLM tool can generate arbitrary-discount coupons
description: The unauthenticated chat endpoint exposes a coupon-generation tool whose only enforcement is an LLM instruction. The tool itself neither authenticates the caller nor verifies a damaged order, rejected return/exchange, one-time use, or the 10% maximum. Its schema accepts any numeric discount and passes it directly to `security.generateCoupon`. An attacker can submit crafted chat messages or otherwise induce the model to call `generateCoupon` with an arbitrary discount, obtaining coupons without satisfying the stated business policy. This is an excessive-agency and server-side authorization failure because the security-critical decision is delegated to the model rather than independently enforced.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat reaches the exported chat handler; the route is registered without authentication middleware, and the caller is outside this file.
The handler accepts caller-controlled `req.body.messages` and supplies them to the model, allowing the caller to influence whether and how the model invokes tools.

The model is given the `generateCoupon` tool and is allowed to make tool calls during up to 10 agent steps. The coupon policy exists only in the system prompt and is not a server-side authorization check.

The tool accepts any numeric `discount` without a maximum check, customer authentication, order verification, return/exchange rejection check, or one-time issuance check, then generates the coupon directly.
The arbitrary discount is passed to `security.generateCoupon`, which creates the attacker-obtainable coupon.

title: User-controlled username is injected into the LLM system prompt
description: A caller-controlled username is interpolated directly into the system prompt as if it were trusted instruction text. A username containing newline-separated instructions can alter the effective system prompt and attempt to override the chatbot's rules, including rules governing tool use. Because the chat endpoint is unauthenticated and the model has a coupon-generation capability, this creates a prompt-injection path to behavior outside the intended store-assistance workflow. The content is not fenced, escaped, or represented as data.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat invokes the chat handler without route-level authentication; the external caller and any username-management path are outside this file.
The handler obtains a username from the request token and database, but no trust boundary or content restriction is applied before using it in the prompt.

`buildSystemPrompt` inserts `userName` into the instruction string using direct interpolation, with no delimiting or escaping that would prevent instruction-like username content from being interpreted by the model.
The resulting prompt is supplied as the model's `system` message alongside tools, so injected username text can attempt to override system rules and influence tool invocation.

title: Unauthenticated chat allows unbounded LLM and tool consumption
description: The public chat endpoint has no rate-limiting, request-size, message-count, or token-budget control visible in this file. It accepts `req.body.messages` wholesale and starts an LLM request, while the model may perform up to 10 agent steps and tool calls. An attacker can repeatedly submit large conversation histories or many requests to consume provider tokens, application CPU, database queries, and concurrent streaming connections. Other infrastructure controls may exist outside this file, but no application-level protection is present here.

trace.description: POST /rest/chat is reachable without authentication or visible per-user/per-IP throttling; the route registration is outside this file.
The handler reads the entire caller-supplied `messages` array without a length, content, token, or conversation-history limit.
The unbounded messages are sent to the LLM with multiple database-backed tools available, and the agent is permitted up to 10 steps per request.

The streaming LLM operation and its tool executions consume provider/API, connection, and database resources for each request; no local timeout, rate limit, or request cost cap is applied at this sink.

title: Raw LLM error details are disclosed through the public chat stream
description: Provider/model errors from the streaming path are sent to the client using the raw `event.error` value rather than the existing `summarizeLlmError` helper. Depending on the provider and SDK error object, this can expose internal endpoint details, request metadata, stack-like diagnostics, or other provider response content to an unauthenticated caller. The catch path is sanitized, but the normal `error` event path is not.

trace.description: The unauthenticated chat endpoint establishes a public streaming response; the route caller is outside this file.
The handler iterates over all provider stream events and handles provider/model failures separately from the sanitized catch path.
For an `error` event, the code interpolates the raw error object into a response payload instead of calling `summarizeLlmError` or applying an allowlist of safe error information.
The raw error is written to the SSE response and therefore reaches the unauthenticated client.

title: Unauthenticated FTP directory browsing and file disclosure
description: The public `/ftp` route enables directory indexing and serves files from the FTP directory without an authentication middleware. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate filenames through the index and download any non-quarantine file exposed there, potentially including backups, uploaded artifacts, or other internal data.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint: unauthenticated requests to GET `/ftp` are routed directly to the FTP directory index.
The same configuration exposes `/ftp(?!/quarantine)/:file` to the public file-serving handler; no authentication or authorization middleware is applied before either the index or file route.

title: Unbounded generated REST collection responses
description: All generated Finale REST resources are configured with `pagination: false`. This includes publicly reachable list endpoints such as `/api/Products` and any other generated collection endpoint not blocked by preceding middleware. A caller can request an unbounded collection, causing the application and database to load and serialize the entire table into memory and the response.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint: generated collection routes such as GET `/api/Products` are created for each model.
The application registers every model in `autoModels` with Finale, including Product and other collection resources.
Finale is explicitly configured with `pagination: false`, so collection requests have no page-size or result-count bound and can return all rows in one request.

title: Unbounded disk-backed file upload
description: The `/rest/memories` upload route uses `uploadToDisk`, but that Multer instance has no file-size, field-count, or file-count limits. The disk storage destination writes the uploaded content into the application’s frontend assets directory. Repeated or very large multipart uploads can exhaust disk space and degrade or stop the service.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint: POST `/rest/memories` accepts a multipart `image` upload and passes it to `uploadToDisk` before the memory and user-ID middleware.
The route uses a disk-backed Multer instance; unlike `uploadToMemory`, the route does not show a size limit or a count limit.

The Multer disk-storage destination writes accepted uploads into `frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/uploads/`, allowing attacker-controlled requests to consume local disk capacity and place files in a served application asset tree.

title: Hardcoded weak cookie-signing secret
description: The application uses the hardcoded string `kekse` as the cookie-signing secret. If any signed cookie is used by the application or its middleware, an attacker who knows this source-visible secret can forge valid signed-cookie values, potentially changing trusted cookie state. The secret is also shared by every deployment using this source configuration.

trace.description: The application initializes cookie parsing as part of its request middleware configuration; the caller is the framework and is outside this file.
The cookie parser is configured with the literal signing secret `kekse` rather than a deployment-specific secret sourced from protected configuration.
Cookie parsing and signature verification therefore rely on a predictable, hardcoded secret that can be used to generate forged signed cookies.

title: Mass assignment on generated Product API
description: The generated Product REST resource accepts the authenticated POST `/api/Products` endpoint, while the resource is configured with an empty exclusion list. Finale therefore binds caller-supplied request properties to the Product model without an explicit allow-list. A caller can submit server-managed Product properties such as pricing, inventory, or privilege/business-state fields if present on the model, bypassing property-level authorization and corrupting product data.

trace.description: Attacker-facing entrypoint: POST `/api/Products` is enabled for any caller satisfying `security.isAuthorized()`; the route does not impose property-level restrictions.
The Product model is registered as an automatic Finale REST resource with `exclude: []`, meaning no Product attributes are excluded from generated create/update binding.

Finale constructs the resource using the model and passes the empty exclusion list as `excludeAttributes`; request body fields are consequently eligible for automatic persistence rather than being restricted to an explicit safe allow-list.
